Theorem 6.9 (schedulable domination)
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses (A1-NS) · Uses 2.1, 3.1, 3.3, 4.3(a), 4.4, 6.1, 6.3

Statement (theory note, §6.2).
Theorem 6.9 (schedulable domination) [SD]. Assume (A1-NS). Let a feasible plan have cost \(C\) and makespan \(M\). Then there are a role configuration on all \(p\) planes with passenger count \(t\) and cost at most \(C\), orders of its drop-offs and pick-ups, and a link matching whose template has makespan at most \(M\). Neither an event order, nor (AΔ), nor (AΔ-path) is needed.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Step 1: a simple plan with clean journeys. Replace central flights and clean, as in the proof of Theorem 6.1; cost, arrival times, flight times and makespan do not increase. By Lemma 4.3(a), every journey is now a leg \(\alpha_\pi : C_I \to x\) followed by a leg \(\beta_\pi : x \to C_G\), which departs no earlier than \(\alpha_\pi\) arrives. Every route is a sequence of segments, one per landing. For a segment \(\gamma\) at a city \(x\), let \(a(\gamma)\) be the time its first leg arrives in \(x\) and \(e(\gamma)\) the time its second leg departs, so \(a(\gamma) \le e(\gamma)\). From here on only the routes and the pairs \((\alpha_\pi, \beta_\pi)\) matter: the moves below keep the routes valid, but need not keep a plan in the sense of item 2 of §1.2.
Step 2: rewiring. Next to the routes, keep a set of loops, empty at first: closed walks whose legs all depart and arrive at one time \(\tau\), so last \(0\), and alternate between hubs and central cities, so that a loop is made of segments too. A passenger is carried through if \(\alpha_\pi\) and \(\beta_\pi\) are the two legs of one segment, of a route or of a loop. Otherwise it is a hand-off, from the segment \(\gamma\) of \(\alpha_\pi\) to the segment \(\gamma'\) of \(\beta_\pi\), both at its city \(x\). While one of these moves applies, apply it.

Exchange. \(\gamma\) is on the route of \(u\), \(\gamma'\) on the route of \(v \ne u\), and \(a(\gamma') \le e(\gamma)\): \(v\) is in \(x\) before \(u\) leaves. Give \(u\) the legs of \(v\) from \(\beta_\pi\) on, and \(v\) the legs of \(u\) after \(\alpha_\pi\). Both routes stay valid: \(\beta_\pi\) departs after \(\alpha_\pi\) arrives, and the second leg of \(\gamma\) departs after the first leg of \(\gamma'\) arrives.
Cut. \(\gamma\) and \(\gamma'\) are on one route, \(\gamma'\) before \(\gamma\). The route gives \(e(\gamma') \le a(\gamma)\) and the journey \(a(\gamma) \le e(\gamma')\), so every leg from \(\beta_\pi\) to \(\alpha_\pi\) departs and arrives at \(\tau = e(\gamma')\) and lasts \(0\); in particular \(d_x = \bar d_x = 0\). These legs form a closed walk at \(x\). Remove it from the route, which keeps the first leg of \(\gamma'\) and the second leg of \(\gamma\), a segment at \(x\) since \(a(\gamma') \le \tau \le e(\gamma)\). The walk becomes a loop; its segments are \((\alpha_\pi, \beta_\pi)\) and the segments strictly between \(\gamma'\) and \(\gamma\).
Splice. One of \(\gamma, \gamma'\) is a segment \(F\) of a loop at time \(\tau\), the other a segment \(\delta\) of a route, and \(e(\gamma) > a(\gamma')\). Then \(a(\delta) < \tau \le e(\delta)\) or \(a(\delta) \le \tau < e(\delta)\): if \(F = \gamma\), then \(e(\gamma) = \tau > a(\delta)\) and \(\tau \le e(\delta)\) by the journey; if \(F = \gamma'\), then \(a(\delta) \le \tau\) by the journey and \(e(\delta) > \tau\). Insert the loop into the route at \(\delta\): the first leg of \(\delta\), the second leg of \(F\), the loop around to \(F\), the first leg of \(F\), the second leg of \(\delta\). The route stays valid, and \(\pi\) is carried through by the new segment of \(\alpha_\pi\) and \(\beta_\pi\).

Every move keeps the legs, so the cost, and every route’s last leg or exchanges two of them, so the makespan. It keeps the routes valid and the loops closed walks at one time, and it carries one more passenger through. It carries none less: the only segments it breaks are \(\gamma\) and \(\gamma'\), and a segment carrying another passenger through holds both of that passenger’s legs, so it is neither. So the moves stop, after at most \(t\) of them. Then every hand-off from \(\gamma\) to \(\gamma'\) has \(e(\gamma) \le a(\gamma')\):

between the routes of two planes, the exchange does not apply, so \(e(\gamma) < a(\gamma')\);
on one route, the cut does not apply, so \(\gamma'\) comes after \(\gamma\), and \(e(\gamma) \le a(\gamma')\) along the route;
between a loop and a route, the splice does not apply;
between two loops, at times \(\tau\) and \(\tau'\): \(e(\gamma) = \tau\) is when \(\alpha_\pi\) arrives and \(a(\gamma') = \tau'\) when \(\beta_\pi\) departs.

Step 3: paths. At each city \(x\), draw an arrow from \(\gamma\) to \(\gamma'\) for each hand-off at \(x\); the segments are those of the routes and of the loops. Each leg carries at most one passenger, so every segment has at most one outgoing and one incoming arrow. A \(B\) has no incoming arrow, since its second leg returns to \(C_I\), which clean journeys never reach, and a \(\bar B\) has no outgoing arrow. So the arrows form disjoint paths \(\gamma_0 \to \gamma_1 \to \dots \to \gamma_m\) with \(m \ge 1\), and cycles. The inner segments of a path, and all segments of a cycle, have an incoming and an outgoing arrow, so they are \(A\) segments, each dropping one passenger and picking up another. Along a path, by step 2, \(a(\gamma_0) \le e(\gamma_0) \le a(\gamma_1) \le \dots \le e(\gamma_m)\).
Step 4: selection. Attach each loop to any plane. Take every \(A\) and \(\bar A\) segment of each plane, on its route and its loops, as a crossing. A route from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\) has \(\#A - \#\bar A = 1\) (Lemma 2.1) and a closed loop \(0\), so each plane gets an odd number of crossings. For each path from a \(B\) to a \(\bar B\), take its \(B\) as a drop-off and its \(\bar B\) as a pick-up, linked to each other. Take no other segment. The balance holds link by link. A passenger carried through rides an \(A\), which carries no arrow; every other passenger is an arrow of exactly one path or cycle. A cycle of \(k\) arrows consists of \(k\) \(A\) segments. A path with \(m\) arrows contributes its \(m - 1\) inner \(A\) segments, one more for each end that is an \(A\), and one link if it runs from a \(B\) to a \(\bar B\): at least \(m\) in every case. So the passenger count, the number of links plus the number of \(A\) segments, is at least \(t\). Distinct segments have distinct first legs, each a leg of the plan of step 1 landing at the segment’s city, so the selected segments are distinct landings of that plan and the cost is at most \(C\). A route segment is simple and lasts its role duration (Lemma 3.3(c)); a loop segment has role duration \(0\), since its legs last \(0\). So \(\lambda_k \le F_k \le M\), where \(F_k\) is the flight time of the rewired route of plane \(k\): it is valid, starts at time \(\ge 0\) and ends by \(M\).
Step 5: the closed form. The closed form \(M_{\rm tmpl}\) of Lemma 6.3 makes sense for any configuration, orders and matching. Order the drop-offs of each plane with those of its loops first, then those of its route in route order, and its pick-ups with those of its route in route order, then those of its loops. Use the links of step 4. Take a link from the \(j\)-th drop-off \(\gamma\) of \(u\) to the \(l\)-th pick-up \(\gamma'\) of \(v\), at \(x\). If \(\gamma\) is on the route, \(u\) flies its earlier route drop-offs before \(\gamma\), and the loop drop-offs weigh \(0\), so \(\mathrm{Pre}_u(j) + d_x \le a(\gamma)\); if \(\gamma\) is in a loop, \(\mathrm{Pre}_u(j) = d_x = 0\). If \(\gamma'\) is on the route, \(v\) flies \(\bar d_x\) to \(C_G\) after \(e(\gamma')\) and then its later route pick-ups, all by time \(M\), and the loop pick-ups weigh \(0\), so \(e(\gamma') + \bar d_x + \mathrm{Suf}_v(l) \le M\); if \(\gamma'\) is in a loop at time \(\tau\), \(\bar d_x = \mathrm{Suf}_v(l) = 0\) and \(e(\gamma') = \tau \le M\): every leg of a loop was a leg of a route before that route’s last leg, which arrives by \(M\). As \(a(\gamma) \le e(\gamma')\) (step 3), the term of the link is at most \(M\). Together with \(\lambda_k \le M\), \(M_{\rm tmpl} \le M\).
Step 6: shrink. Lemma 4.4 (\(t \ge p\), §1.1) brings the passenger count to \(t\), deleting two crossings of a plane or a drop-off together with a pick-up at its city. Take the pick-up linked to it, so that the remaining links still match drop-offs and pick-ups city by city. With the same orders, deleting crossings only lowers loads, and deleting a link lowers loads and the \(\mathrm{Pre}\) and \(\mathrm{Suf}\) of the other links, so \(M_{\rm tmpl}\) stays at most \(M\). The configuration now has passenger count \(t\), and by Lemma 6.3 its template has makespan \(M_{\rm tmpl} \le M\). \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





The previous version of this proof kept a feasible, event-ordered plan through step 2. It exchanged only the hand-offs that overlap in the event order, so it needed one, and it left open plans that are not event-ordered on instances with a city of \(d_x = \bar d_x = 0\). On such a plan an exchange could leave a journey whose two legs lie on one plane in the wrong order. The cut handles exactly that case: the two legs and everything between them happen at one instant, at a city with \(d_x = \bar d_x = 0\), and the template does not need them in the plan’s order, since their segments weigh nothing. checks/sd_zero_check.py runs the three moves and steps 3 to 6 on random plans of this kind (§11).

Steps 3–6 run with the remaining loops attached to one plane (withLoops). not_schedulableDomination shows that the hypothesis p ≤ t is needed.

Corollary 6.10 (non-symmetric front)

Corollary 6.10 (non-symmetric front). Assume (A1-NS). Let \(m(\mathrm{cfg})\) be the least makespan of a role configuration (§6.2), let \[\mathcal K = \{(c(\mathrm{cfg}),\ m(\mathrm{cfg})) : \mathrm{cfg} \text{ a role configuration on the } p \text{ planes with passenger count } t\},\] and let \(\mathcal A_{\rm eo} \subseteq \mathcal A\) be the set of points of feasible event-ordered plans. title: Blueprint

The exact algorithm (symmetric case)
§7 of the note turns Corollary 4.8 into a pseudo-polynomial algorithm: the front is the set of breakpoints of \(E(T)\), the least cost of an admissible partition with loads at most \(T\). Both exact dynamic programs are proved equal to \(E(T)\) in Lean, and the verified solver zeno-front is built on them.

Proposition 7.1
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses (S), (A1) · Uses 4.8

Statement (theory note, §7.1).
Proposition 7.1. Under (S) and (A1), \(\mathcal F = \{(E(T), 2T) : T \in \mathbb N,\ E(T) < E(T-1)\}\) with \(E(-1) = \infty\), makespans in units of \(g\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Here \(M(X)\) is an even integer and \(E(T) = \min\{c(X) : M(X) \le 2T\}\). Let \((c, 2T) \in \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal X\) (Corollary 4.8). Then \(c = E(T)\), otherwise a cheaper \(X\) with \(M(X) \le 2T\) dominates it; and \(E(T-1) > c\), otherwise some \(X\) with \(c(X) \le c\) and \(M(X) < 2T\) dominates it. Conversely, let \(E(T) < E(T-1)\) and let \(X\) attain \(E(T)\); then \(M(X) = 2T\). A point \((c(Y), M(Y)) \in \mathcal X\) dominating it has \(M(Y) \le 2T\), hence \(M(Y) = 2T\) (otherwise \(c(Y) \ge E(T-1) > E(T)\)), and then \(c(Y) = E(T)\). \(\square\)



In Lean. minimal_admissiblePoints_iff: (C, 2T) is a minimal admissible point iff E(T) = C and E(T') > C for every T' < T; with Corollary 4.8 this is the proposition.

Proposition 7.3. \(L(T) \le E(T) \le U_3(T) \le U(T)\).

Proposition 7.4
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 2.6, 2.7, 7.3

Statement (theory note, §7.3).
Proposition 7.4. If \(q_{\max} \le 2\), that is \(p \le 2\) or \(t \le p + 1\), then \(E = U\). If \(q_{\max} \le 3\), that is \(p \le 3\) or \(t \le p + 2\), then \(E = U_3\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Take \(X\) attaining \(E(T)\) and a link forest (Lemma 2.6). Its trees have at most \(q_{\max}\) planes (Corollary 2.7), and trees with 1, 2 or 3 vertices are a vertex, an edge and a path. In each, a group consists of its link copies and a filler of the size and budget used in the gadget formula, whose cost is at least the corresponding \(G\) value (Lemma 7.2). So the forest costs at least some combination of gadgets. \(\square\)






Theorem 7.5
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Uses 2.6, 2.7, 7.2

Statement (theory note, §7.4).
Theorem 7.5. \(\mathrm{For}[p][s] = E(T)\). Given \(G\), the computation takes \(O(n\,q_{\max}^2 s^2 T + p\,q_{\max} s^2)\) time and \(O(q_{\max} s T + n q_{\max} s + p s)\) memory per level.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. A rooted structure is a rooted tree on \(q\) planes with city-labelled edges and a group \(X_u\) for each plane, such that the edges at \(u\) have distinct copies in \(X_u\) (F1), \(r_u = |X_u| - \deg(u)\) is odd and \(\delta(X_u) \le T\). In a hanging structure with label \(a\), the root’s group holds one more copy of \(a\), counted in its degree and its duration. Each group splits into its link copies and its free landings, of odd size \(r_u\).
(\(\ge\)) By induction on \(q\), every finite entry is the cost of a structure of its kind, with \(G\)-optimal free landings (Lemma 7.2): \(\mathrm{Sub}_a\) and \(\mathrm{Root}\) add a root with \(r\) free landings within the remaining budget to a multiset of child items, and \(\mathrm{Ch}_q\) adds one item to a multiset of items. The forest behind \(\mathrm{For}[p][s]\) satisfies (F1)–(F2) and has \(p\) planes, \(s\) landings and groups of duration at most \(T\), so it is admissible by Lemma 2.6, and \(\mathrm{For}[p][s] \ge E(T)\).
(\(\le\)) Take \(X\) attaining \(E(T)\) and a link forest (Lemma 2.6); its trees have at most \(q_{\max}\) planes (Corollary 2.7). Root each tree. By induction on subtree size: the child items of a plane \(u\) cost at least \(\mathrm{Ch}_{q-1}[\tau_u][j']\), where \(\tau_u\) sums \(d_b\) over the child links of \(u\) (remove one item and bound its subtree by \(\mathrm{Sub}_b\)); the free landings of \(u\) have size \(r_u\) and duration at most \(T - \tau_u\), less \(d_a\) for a hanging root, so they cost at least the matching \(G\) entry. So each subtree costs at least its \(\mathrm{Sub}\) or \(\mathrm{Root}\) entry, and the forest at least \(\mathrm{For}[p][s]\).
Complexity. \(\mathrm{Ch}\) has \(q_{\max}(T+1)(s+1)\) entries, each a minimum over \(b\), \(q'\) and \(j'\), which is \(O(n\,q_{\max} s)\). \(\mathrm{Sub}\) and \(\mathrm{Root}\) range over \(q\), \(a\), \(\tau\), \(j'\) and \(r\): \(O(n\,q_{\max} T s^2)\). \(\mathrm{For}\) costs \(O(p\,q_{\max} s^2)\). \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





Over the levels \([T_{\rm lo}, T_{\rm hi}]\) of Proposition 7.10, with \(G\) built once in \(O(n\,s\,T_{\rm hi})\), the whole front takes \(O(n\,q_{\max}^2 s^2\, T_{\rm hi}(T_{\rm hi} - T_{\rm lo} + 1))\) time. This is pseudo-polynomial, since \(T_{\rm hi} \le d_{\max}\kappa\).

Theorem 7.6 (σ-DP)
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Uses 2.2, 2.8, 7.2

Statement (theory note, §7.5).
Theorem 7.6 (σ-DP) [Claim C]. The shortest path from \((0, 0, \emptyset)\) to \((p, s, \emptyset)\) has weight \(E(T)\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Paths give admissible partitions. Take a path with options \((m_k, \eta_k)\). Let \(R_k\) be a \(G\)-optimal \((m_k - |\eta_k|)\)-multiset within \(T - \delta(\eta_k)\) and \(X_k = \eta_k + R_k\). Then \(|X| = s\), \(\delta(X_k) \le T\), and \(h_{k,i} = [i \in \eta_k]\) is a parity matrix: (h1) as \(\eta_k \le X_k\); (h2) as \(|\eta_k| \equiv m_k + 1\); (h3) because the final \(\sigma = \eta_1 \triangle \dots \triangle \eta_p\) is empty, so every city lies in an even number of the \(\eta_k\). So the path’s weight is at least \(E(T)\).
Admissible partitions give paths. Take \(X\) attaining \(E(T)\) and a parity matrix touching at most \(w\) cities (Lemma 2.8(c)). With the options \((|X_k|, \eta_k)\), every prefix \(\sigma_k = \eta_1 \triangle \dots \triangle \eta_k \subseteq Z(h)\) has at most \(w\) cities, \(|\eta_k| \le \min(|X_k| - 1, w)\), and \(R_k = X_k - \eta_k\) costs at least \(G[|X_k| - |\eta_k|][T - \delta(\eta_k)]\). So some path has weight at most \(c(X)\). \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





Size. An arc joins sets \(\sigma, \sigma'\) with \(|\sigma|, |\sigma'|, |\sigma \triangle \sigma'| \le w\), so \(|\sigma \cup \sigma'| \le \lfloor 3w/2\rfloor\); there are at most \(N_w = \sum_{u \le \lfloor 3w/2\rfloor} \binom{n}{u} 3^u\) such pairs. The DP takes \(O(p\,s\,\hat m\,N_w)\) time per level: polynomial in \(n\) for fixed \(w\), practical only for small \(w\) or few cities. The link-forest DP is the default otherwise.



In Lean. The σ-DP’s states are restricted to subsets of the non-dominated cities of size at most min(p − 1, t − p) (Lemma 2.8); every finite value is attained by groups whose witness sets form a parity witness, so no link forest is needed.

Lemma 7.7 (Pareto sets)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 1.1, 7.6

Statement (theory note, §7.5).
Lemma 7.7 (Pareto sets). Let \(\otimes\) be a binary operation on \(\mathbb K^2\) that is monotone in the product order. For finite \(A\) and \(B\), \(\mathrm{Min}(A \otimes B) = \mathrm{Min}(\mathrm{Min}\,A \otimes \mathrm{Min}\,B)\) and \(\mathrm{Min}(A \cup B) = \mathrm{Min}(\mathrm{Min}\,A \cup \mathrm{Min}\,B)\), where \(A \otimes B = \{a \otimes b : a \in A, b \in B\}\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Every \(a \in A\) is weakly dominated by some \(a^\star \in \mathrm{Min}\,A\) (finiteness), so \(a \otimes b\) is weakly dominated by \(a^\star \otimes b^\star \in \mathrm{Min}\,A \otimes \mathrm{Min}\,B \subseteq A \otimes B\). This subset is finite and dominating, and Lemma 1.1 applies. The same argument works for \(\cup\). \(\square\)






Proposition 7.8 (Pareto-set variant)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 1.1, 7.6

Statement (theory note, §7.5).
Proposition 7.8 (Pareto-set variant) [PS]. In the σ-graph, replace the weight of the arc with option \((m, \eta)\) by the finite set \(\mathrm{Opt}(m, \eta) = \mathrm{Min}\{(c(\eta) + G[m - |\eta|][\tau],\ \delta(\eta) + \tau) : 0 \le \tau \le T_{\rm hi} - \delta(\eta)\}\). Combine along paths with \((c, \tau) \otimes (c', \tau') = (c + c', \max(\tau, \tau'))\), and keep at each node the \(\mathrm{Min}\) over its incoming arcs. The set obtained at \((p, s, \emptyset)\) is \(\mathrm{Min}\{(c(X), \max_k \delta(X_k)) : |X| = s,\ X_1,\dots,X_p \text{ admissible},\ \max_k \delta(X_k) \le T_{\rm hi}\}\). Under (S) and (A1) its points \((c, \tau)\) are the front points \((c, 2\tau)\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. \(\otimes\) is monotone. \(\mathrm{Opt}(m, \eta)\) is the \(\mathrm{Min}\) of the points \((c(\eta) + c(R), \delta(\eta) + \delta(R))\) over all \(R\) of size \(m - |\eta|\) within the budget: each such point is weakly dominated by the term with \(\tau = \delta(R)\), and each term is attained or weakly dominated by a \(G\)-optimal \(R\). By Lemma 7.7 and induction over the layers, each node holds the \(\mathrm{Min}\) of the points of all paths reaching it, with arbitrary fillers. By both directions of Theorem 7.6 (with any filler in place of the \(G\)-optimal one, and the restriction \(w\) being independent of the level), these are exactly the points of admissible partitions with \(|X| = s\). The front statement is Corollary 4.8, and every front point has \(\tau \le T_{\rm hi}\) (Proposition 7.10). \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





Combining sets is no better than sweeping the levels in the worst case. It helps when durations are large and the cost range is narrow.






Proposition 7.9 (dominance)
Lean informal (parts in Lean) · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses — ; fronts: (S), (A1) · Uses 2.2, 7.1

Statement (theory note, §7.6).
Proposition 7.9 (dominance) [DOM]. Let \(i \ne i'\) with \(d_{i'} \le d_i\) and \(c_{i'} \le c_i\). Removing city \(i\) leaves \(E(T)\) and \(L(T)\) unchanged at every \(T\). Under (S) and (A1), it leaves the front unchanged.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Removing a city can only raise \(E\) and \(L\). Conversely, in an optimal \(X\) and its groups, replace every copy of \(i\) by \(i'\): costs and durations do not increase. Nothing else is needed for \(L\). For \(E\), set \(h'_{k,i'} = (h_{k,i} + h_{k,i'}) \bmod 2\) and \(h'_{k,i} = 0\). Row sums keep their parity, column \(i'\) is the sum of two even columns, and \(h'_{k,i'} = 1\) means \(X_k\) contained \(i\) or \(i'\), so the new group contains \(i'\). The instance without \(i\) still satisfies (S) and (A1), and Proposition 7.1 expresses both fronts through \(E\). \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





Applied repeatedly: keep one city per class of equal \((d, c)\), and drop every city dominated by another.

Proposition 7.10 (ends of the front)
Lean informal (parts in Lean) · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses (S) · Uses 2.9, 3.2, 3.4, 4.1

Statement (theory note, §7.6).
Proposition 7.10 (ends of the front) [END]. Assume (S). Let \(d_{\min} = \min_i d_i\), \(c_{\min} = \min_i c_i\) and \(d_{\rm cheap} = \min\{d_i : c_i = c_{\min}\}\).

Every plan has makespan at least \(M_1 := 2d_{\min}\kappa\), and some plan has makespan \(M_1\).
Every plan costs at least \(s\,c_{\min}\). A plan of cost \(s\,c_{\min}\) has makespan at least \(M_r := 2d_{\rm cheap}\kappa\), and some plan has cost \(s\,c_{\min}\) and makespan \(M_r\). So \((s\,c_{\min}, M_r)\) is the cheapest point of \(\mathcal F\), and every point of \(\mathcal F\) has makespan at least \(M_1\).
With integer durations, \(E(T) < \infty\) iff \(T \ge T_{\rm lo} := d_{\min}\kappa\), and \(E(T) = s\,c_{\min}\) iff \(T \ge T_{\rm hi} := d_{\rm cheap}\kappa\). The same holds for \(L\).

No assumption on central flights is needed, and zero durations and ties are covered. The cost of the first point is not in closed form; under (A1) it is \(E(T_{\rm lo})\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Pigeonhole: \(p\) non-empty groups of total size \(s\) include one of size at least \(\kappa\).

Lemma 3.4 gives such groups with \(\ell(Y_k) \le M\), so \(M \ge 2d_{\min}\kappa\). For the plan, put \(s\) copies of a city of duration \(d_{\min}\) into groups of sizes \(\lfloor s/p\rfloor\) and \(\lceil s/p\rceil\), all non-empty as \(s \ge p\). This is admissible by Lemma 2.9 (\(s \equiv p\), one city), and Theorem 4.1 gives a plan of makespan \(2d_{\min}\kappa\).
By Lemma 3.2 there are at least \(s\) central landings, each costing at least \(c_{\min}\). If \(C = s\,c_{\min}\), the multiset \(Y\) of Lemma 3.4 has \(c(Y) \le s\,c_{\min}\) and \(|Y| = s\), so all its cities cost \(c_{\min}\) and have \(d \ge d_{\rm cheap}\); pigeonhole gives \(M \ge 2d_{\rm cheap}\kappa\). The plan is that of (a) built on a cheapest city of duration \(d_{\rm cheap}\). A point \((C, M) \in \mathcal A\) weakly dominating \((s\,c_{\min}, M_r)\) has \(C = s\,c_{\min}\), hence \(M \ge M_r\).
The same arguments apply to \(E\) and \(L\) directly: every partition has a group of size at least \(\kappa\), and the single-city partitions are admissible. \(\square\)










Remarks in the note





Only the levels \([T_{\rm lo}, T_{\rm hi}]\) need computing. On generator instances this range is about ten times shorter than \([0, d_{\max}\hat m]\).



In Lean. The two lower bounds the checker uses (obligations 2 and 4): every plan has makespan at least 2 d_min ⌈s/p⌉ and cost at least s c_min. The attainment half is not formalized.

title: Blueprint
text:
Complexity
§8 explains why no fast per-PPP rule can be exact, and why the dynamic programs are pseudo-polynomial. None of it is formalized.

Theorem 8.1
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses \(p\) in the input · Uses 2.4

Statement (theory note, §8).
Theorem 8.1. Deciding \(M(X) \le 2T\), with \(d\), \(X\), \(p\) and \(T\) as input, is strongly NP-complete.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Membership: guess the partition and a parity matrix, and check Definition 2.2. Hardness, from 3-Partition, which is strongly NP-complete: given integers \(a_1,\dots,a_{3m}\) with \(B/4 < a_i < B/2\) and \(\sum_i a_i = mB\), can they be split into \(m\) triples of sum \(B\)? Take \(3m\) cities with \(d_i = a_i\), \(p = m\) and \(t = 2m\) (so \(s = 3m\)), \(X\) containing every city once, and \(T = B\). Each city lies in one group, so every component of \(H\) is one plane with its cities, and admissibility makes every group odd (Lemma 2.4). A 3-partition gives \(m\) triples, odd groups of duration \(B\). Conversely, groups of duration at most \(B\) summing to \(mB\) all have duration exactly \(B\); a group of one or two items has duration below \(B\) and one of four or more above \(B\), so all groups are triples. The numbers are those of the 3-Partition instance, so the reduction preserves strong NP-hardness. \(\square\)






Proposition 8.2 (fixed \(p\))
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 2.2, 2.4

Statement (theory note, §8).
Proposition 8.2 (fixed \(p\)). For \(p = 2\) the problem stays NP-complete, even with positive durations. For every fixed \(p\) it is solvable in time polynomial in \(n\), \(s\) and \(T\). So for fixed \(p\) it is weakly NP-complete.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Hardness, from Partition: given \(a_1,\dots,a_m\) with sum \(2B\), is there a subset of sum \(B\)? Choose an odd \(r \ge m\), add \(2r - m\) zero items, and give each of the \(2r\) items its own city of duration \(a_i + K\), with \(K = B + 1\). Let \(p = 2\), \(t = r + 1\) (so \(s = 2r\)) and \(T = B + rK\). Distinct cities make both groups odd (Lemma 2.4). If a subset of sum \(B\) exists, pad both sides with zero items to \(r\) items each, which \(r \ge m\) allows: two odd groups of duration \(B + rK\). Conversely, the two groups have duration exactly \(B + rK\) each, since they sum to \(2B + 2rK\). A group with \(r + 1\) items or more has duration at least \((r+1)K > B + rK\), so both groups have \(r\) items, and the original items of one of them sum to \(B\).
Algorithm for fixed \(p\): process the cities one at a time, with states made of the group durations (each in \([0, T]\)), the parities of \(|X_k|\) and of \(h_k\), and whether each group is non-empty: \((T+1)^p 8^p\) states. For city \(i\), choose how its \(X(i)\) copies split among the planes (\(O(s^{p-1})\) ways), and an even set of planes that received a copy, on which \(h_{k,i} = 1\) (at most \(2^{p-1}\) ways). Conditions (h1) and (h3) are local to the city, and (h2) is checked at the end. The time is \(O(n\,(T+1)^p\, 8^p\, s^{p-1}\, 2^p)\). \(\square\)






Corollary 8.3
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 7.5

Statement (theory note, §8).
Corollary 8.3. \(E(T)\), and under (S) and (A1) the front, are computable in pseudo-polynomial time (Theorem 7.5). So computing the front is not strongly NP-hard unless P = NP. Whether deciding \(E(T) \le C\) is NP-hard, with \(t\) in unary as in PDDL, is not established here.

title: Blueprint
text:
Certificates
§9: a certificate lists one plan per point and one lower bound per gap; four obligations imply that the list is the front. The Lean checker is the executable form of Theorem 9.1, and its soundness theorems are the strongest machine-checked results of the project.

Theorem 9.1 (end to end)
Lean machine-checked · Note proof in the note · Uses 1.1

Statement (theory note, §9).
Theorem 9.1 (end to end) [X3]. If obligations 1–4 hold, then \(\mathcal F = \{(C_i, M_i) : 1 \le i \le r\}\).






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Let \((C, M) \in \mathcal A\). By 2, \(M \ge M_1\). Let \(i\) be the largest index with \(M_i \le M\). If \(i < r\), then \(M < M_{i+1}\) and \(C \ge C_i\) by 3; if \(i = r\), then \(C \ge C_r\) by 4. Either way \((C_i, M_i) \preceq (C, M)\). So the list, contained in \(\mathcal A\) by 1, is a finite dominating subset, and by Lemma 1.1, \(\mathcal F\) is its \(\mathrm{Min}\). That is the whole list, which is strictly monotone in both coordinates. \(\square\)



In Lean. Cert.check_sound: if check accepts, the listed points are exactly the Pareto front of every feasible plan, for every table of central flights satisfying (A1), or every table if all gaps are relaxed. Cert.check_sound_rat extends it to plans with rational times and Cert.check_sound_anywhere to planes ending anywhere.

Lemma 9.2 (potentials)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 7.6

Statement (theory note, §9).
Lemma 9.2 (potentials) [X2]. In a finite graph with arc weights in \(\mathbb K\), let \(V\) map nodes to \(\mathbb K \cup \{\infty\}\) with \(V(\text{target}) \le 0\) and \(V(u) \le \mathrm{wt}(u,v) + V(v)\) on every arc. Then \(V(\text{source})\) is at most the weight of every path from the source to the target.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. Along a path \(u_0, \dots, u_m\) ending at the target, \(V(u_m) \le 0\), and by backward induction \(V(u_j) \le \sum_{j' \ge j} \mathrm{wt}(u_{j'}, u_{j'+1})\). \(\square\)






Lemma 9.3 (default potentials)
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Uses 7.6

Statement (theory note, §9).
Lemma 9.3 (default potentials). At level \(T\), let \(G^a[m] = c_a + G[m-1][T - d_a]\), the cheapest \(m\)-group containing \(a\). Let \(L_{\rm rest}(p, s) = 0\), \(L_{\rm rest}(p, j) = \infty\) for \(j \ne s\), and \(L_{\rm rest}(k, j) = \min_m \big(G[m][T] + L_{\rm rest}(k+1, j+m)\big)\). Let \(L^a(p, j) = \infty\) and \(L^a(k, j) = \min_m \min\big(G^a[m] + L_{\rm rest}(k+1, j+m),\ G[m][T] + L^a(k+1, j+m)\big)\). Define \(V_0(k, j, \emptyset) = L_{\rm rest}(k, j)\) and \(V_0(k, j, \sigma) = \max_{a\in\sigma} L^a(k, j)\) for \(\sigma \ne \emptyset\). Then \(V_0(\text{target}) = 0\) and \(V_0(u) \le \mathrm{wt}(u, v) + V_0(v)\) on every arc of the σ-graph.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. By induction from \(k = p\), \(L^a \ge L_{\rm rest}\), since \(G^a[m] \ge G[m][T]\); so \(V_0(v) \ge L_{\rm rest}(v)\) at every node \(v\). An arc leaving \((k, j, \sigma)\) with option \((m, \eta)\) has weight at least \(G[m][T]\), and at least \(G^a[m]\) when \(a \in \eta\), because \(\eta\) with its filler is an \(m\)-group of duration at most \(T\). If \(\sigma = \emptyset\): \(V_0(u) = L_{\rm rest}(k, j) \le G[m][T] + L_{\rm rest}(k+1, j+m) \le \mathrm{wt} + V_0(v)\). If \(\sigma \ne \emptyset\) and \(a \in \sigma\): when \(a \in \eta\), \(L^a(k, j) \le G^a[m] + L_{\rm rest}(k+1, j+m) \le \mathrm{wt} + V_0(v)\); when \(a \notin \eta\), \(a \in \sigma \triangle \eta\), so \(V_0(v) \ge L^a(k+1, j+m)\) and \(L^a(k, j) \le G[m][T] + L^a(k+1, j+m) \le \mathrm{wt} + V_0(v)\). Take the maximum over \(a\). \(\square\)









Remarks in the note





Sparse potential. The certificate lists some nodes \(u\) with values \(V(u)\). The checker sets \(V'(u) = \max(V(u), V_0(u))\) on listed nodes and \(V' = V_0\) elsewhere. It checks \(V'(\text{target}) \le 0\), \(V'(u) \le \mathrm{wt}(u, v) + V'(v)\) on every arc leaving a listed node, and \(V'(\text{source}) \ge C_i\). Arcs leaving other nodes satisfy the inequality by Lemma 9.3, as \(V' \ge V_0\). By Lemma 9.2 and Theorem 7.6, \(E(T^\star_i) \ge C_i\). The listed nodes are those that survive the solver’s pruning.

title: Blueprint
text:
The linear family (default generator)
The generator’s default instances have costs affine in durations. §10 gives their front in closed form, which is why the published benchmark fronts are probably right despite the greedy.

Theorem 10.1
Lean informal · Note proof in the note · Hypotheses (S) · Uses 1.1, 2.9, 3.4, 4.1, 7.2, 7.10

Statement (theory note, §10).
Theorem 10.1. Assume (S), \(d_i = i\) and \(c_i = \alpha - \beta i\) for \(i = 1,\dots,n\), with \(\beta \ge 0\) and \(\alpha \ge \beta n\). Let \(q_0 = \lfloor s/p\rfloor\) and \(\rho = s - pq_0\). For every integer \(T \ge \kappa\), \[L(T) = E(T) = \alpha s - \beta\,\Phi(T), \qquad \Phi(T) = (p - \rho)\min(T,\ nq_0) + \rho\min(T,\ n(q_0+1)),\] and \(L(T) = E(T) = \infty\) for \(T < \kappa\). Consequently, whatever the central flights, the front is \[\mathcal F = \{(\alpha s - \beta\,\Phi(T),\ 2T) : \kappa \le T \le n\kappa\} \text{ if } \beta > 0, \qquad
\mathcal F = \{(\alpha s,\ 2\kappa)\} \text{ if } \beta = 0,\] with makespans in units of \(r_0\). For \(\beta > 0\) it has \((n-1)\kappa + 1\) points.






Proof (theory note)





Proof. (1) Affine cost. \(c(Y) = \alpha |Y| - \beta\,\delta(Y)\). An \(m\)-multiset of cities can have any duration in \([m, nm]\): start from \(m\) copies of city 1 and raise one landing by one at a time. So by Lemma 7.2, \(G[m][T] = \alpha m - \beta\min(T, nm)\) for \(1 \le m \le T\), and \(G[m][T] = \infty\) for \(m > T\).

Convexity. \(m \mapsto \min(T, nm)\) is concave, so \(m \mapsto G[m][T]\) is convex on \([1, T]\). A sum \(\sum_k G[m_k][T]\) with \(\sum_k m_k = s\) is then minimised by the balanced profile, with \(p - \rho\) groups of size \(q_0\) and \(\rho\) of size \(q_0 + 1\): if \(m_u \ge m_v + 2\), moving one landing from \(u\) to \(v\) does not increase the sum. The profile is feasible iff \(\kappa \le T\); otherwise \(L = E = \infty\) by Proposition 7.10(c). So \(L(T) = \sum_k G[m_k][T] = \alpha s - \beta\,\Phi(T)\).
Admissibility. Give every group of size \(m\) the same \(G\)-optimal multiset. Exactly one of \(q_0\) and \(q_0 + 1\) is even, so all even groups are equal, and Lemma 2.9 makes the partition admissible. It costs \(L(T)\), so \(E(T) \le L(T) \le E(T)\).
Front. By Lemma 3.4 a plan with makespan \(M\) costs at least \(L(\lfloor M/2\rfloor) = E(\lfloor M/2\rfloor)\), and Theorem 4.1 achieves \((E(T), 2T)\); both need only (S). \(E\) is constant from \(n\kappa\) on, so the finite set \(\{(E(T), 2T) : \kappa \le T \le n\kappa\} \subseteq \mathcal A\) dominates \(\mathcal A\), and Lemma 1.1 gives \(\mathcal F\). For \(\kappa < T \le n\kappa\), \(\Phi(T) - \Phi(T-1)\) is \(p\) when \(T \le nq_0\) and \(\rho\) when \(nq_0 < T \le n(q_0+1)\); the second range meets \([\kappa, n\kappa]\) only if \(\rho \ge 1\). So for \(\beta > 0\) every such \(T\) is a breakpoint. \(\square\)










Remarks in the note





The count \((n-1)\kappa + 1\) matches the front sizes measured with the prototype on generator instances: 1,090 points for \(n = 100\), \(t = 60\), \(p = 10\); 540 for \(n = 50\) with the same \(t\) and \(p\); 399 for \(n = 200\), \(t = 3\), \(p = 2\). Neither link structures nor smoothing the free landings of a group are needed for this family.
What the theorem does not cover:

Offset progressions. For \(d_i = a + bi\) with \(a > 0\), \(G[\cdot][T]\) need not be convex and \(L < E\) occurs. With \(d = (5, 7, 9, 11)\), \(c_i = 24 - 2d_i\), \(t = 7\) and \(p = 4\), \(L(20) = 80 < E(20) = 84\) (by enumeration; 4 of 5,904 levels on 150 random offset instances). Contiguity from the step is essential: the two-city instance \(d = (6, 10)\) of §5 is affine as well.
Conjecture 10.2. The papers’ per-PPP greedy reaches the front of Theorem 10.1. Evidence: equal fronts on 115 instances with \(n \le 6\), \(p \le 5\) and \(s \le 11\). Correctness does not depend on it, since the front is in closed form.
The other generator families (logarithm, square root, \(2^i\), \((5/2)i\)) have no closed form; the general algorithm applies.







Conjecture 10.2
Lean informal · Note open problem · Hypotheses (S), (A1)

Statement (theory note, §10).
Conjecture 10.2. The papers’ per-PPP greedy reaches the front of Theorem 10.1. Evidence: equal fronts on 115 instances with \(n \le 6\), \(p \le 5\) and \(s \le 11\). Correctness does not depend on it, since the front is in closed form.

title: Instances with known fronts
text: Some instances have fronts known independently of zeno: in closed form, or computed by an exhaustive oracle. They are the natural test cases for a planner or another solver.

title: Instances with known fronts
text:
The linear family (default generator)
With the default options (-C 3 -D 3) and -r r, after the 2016 swap, the generator builds \(d_i = r\,i\) and \(c_i = r\,(n + 1 - i)\) for \(i = 1, \dots, n\): cost is affine and decreasing in duration. Theorem 10.1 of the note gives the front in closed form. Let \(s = 2t - p\), \(\kappa = \lceil s/p \rceil\), \(q_0 = \lfloor s/p \rfloor\), \(\rho = s - p q_0\), and \[\Phi(T) = (p - \rho)\min(T,\ n q_0) + \rho \min(T,\ n(q_0 + 1)).\] Then the front is \[\mathcal F = \big\{\big(r\,((n+1)\,s - \Phi(T)),\ 2rT\big) : \kappa \le T \le n\kappa\big\},\] with \((n - 1)\kappa + 1\) points, every \(T\) in the range being a breakpoint. The theorem needs only (S): the front is the same whatever the central flights, and every certificate of this family has only relaxed gaps. In general, the theorem covers \(d_i = i\) and \(c_i = \alpha - \beta i\) with \(\beta > 0\) and \(\alpha \ge \beta n\).
The same in Python, by increasing cost as zeno prints it:
def linear_front(n, t, p, r=1):
    """Front of zeno -n n -t t -p p -r r (default generator), Theorem 10.1."""
    s = 2 * t - p
    q0, rho = divmod(s, p)
    kappa = -(-s // p)
    phi = lambda T: (p - rho) * min(T, n * q0) + rho * min(T, n * (q0 + 1))
    return sorted((r * ((n + 1) * s - phi(T)), 2 * r * T) for T in range(kappa, n * kappa + 1))
It agrees with zeno point for point on, among others, -n 10 -t 8 -p 3 (46 points), -n 7 -t 5 -p 4 (13), -n 5 -t 9 -p 4 -r 3 (17), -n 20 -t 6 -p 2 -r 7 (96) and -n 12 -t 13 -p 5 (56). The note’s own check compared the closed form with the link-forest DP on 336 instances and 5,844 levels.
The count matches the suite: the regimes instances have fronts of 399 (\(n = 200\), \(t = 3\), \(p = 2\)), 540 (\(n = 50\), \(t = 30\), \(p = 5\)) and 1,090 points (\(n = 100\), \(t = 60\), \(p = 10\)), each \((n-1)\kappa + 1\).

Table 1 of EvoCOP 2015: -n N -t N -p 2
For \(n = t = N\) and \(p = 2\): \(s = 2N - 2\), \(\kappa = q_0 = N - 1\) and \(\rho = 0\), so \(\Phi(T) = 2T\) on the range and \[\mathcal F = \{(2(N^2 - 1) - 2T,\ 2T) : N - 1 \le T \le N(N-1)\}.\] Every point has cost + makespan \(= 2(N^2 - 1)\). The front runs from \((2N(N-1),\ 2(N-1))\), the fastest, to \((2(N-1),\ 2N(N-1))\), the cheapest, and has exactly \[(N-1)^2 + 1 \text{ points}.\] That is the front size of Table 1 of the EvoCOP 2015 paper, and zeno reproduces it for every \(N\) up to 50 (2,402 points at \(N = 50\)). What the closed form does not cover

Offset progressions \(d_i = a + bi\) with \(a > 0\): \(G\) need not be convex and \(L < E\) occurs. With \(d = (5, 7, 9, 11)\), \(c_i = 24 - 2d_i\), \(t = 7\) and \(p = 4\), \(L(20) = 80 < E(20) = 84\).

title: Instances with known fronts
text:
The ends of every front
Whatever the family, under (S), Proposition 7.10 fixes the two ends of the front:

the fastest makespan is \(M_1 = 2\,d_{\min}\,\kappa\);
the cheapest cost is \(s\,c_{\min}\), reached first at makespan \(2\,d_{\rm cheap}\,\kappa\), where \(d_{\rm cheap}\) is the shortest duration among the cheapest cities.

Certificates rely on both (obligations 2 and 4 of the format).

title: Instances with known fronts
text:
Small instances with checked fronts

The 27 golden instances (suites): fronts of the exhaustive oracle, in tests/golden/fronts/.
The LPT counterexample, \(d = (6, 10)\), \(c = (40, 20)\), \(t = 5\), \(p = 2\): six points, (160, 80), (200, 72), (240, 64), (260, 60), (280, 56) and (320, 48). The 2016 greedy misses (260, 60). This front is proved in Lean by the kernel alone, for every table of central flights (Examples.lptCounterexample_front, §5).
Proposition 6.5, non-symmetric: \(d = (3, 19)\), \(\bar d = (3, 11)\), \(c = (5, 1)\), \(t = 7\), \(p = 4\), no central flights. The front is (10, 90), (14, 74), (18, 68), (22, 66), (26, 52), (34, 42), (38, 36), (42, 30), (50, 18), as (cost, makespan). An exhaustive search over all plans (937 million states) gives the same front. It is the instance on which waiting is harmful: the role-load bound alone stays below the front, and two of its gaps are closed only by the search kind (Proposition 6.5).
Zero costs, \(n = 1\), \(d_1 = 1\), \(c_1 = 0\), \(t = 5\), \(p = 3\): the front is the single point (0, 6), and plans with more than \(s\) landings also reach it (the remark under Corollary 4.8).

title: PDDL
text: MultiZenoTravel was designed as a benchmark for multi-objective temporal planners. zeno pddl writes any instance as a PDDL 2.1 problem for the domain in pddl/, with its exact front as comments, so that a planner’s output can be scored against the true front.

title: PDDL
text:
The domain
pddl/multi-zeno-travel.pddl (PDDL 2.1 level 3: durative actions and numeric fluents), as it stands in the repository:
; MultiZenoTravel domain (PDDL 2.1, level 3: durative actions and numeric fluents).
;
; Cities: city0 is the initial city C_I, city1..cityN are the central cities,
; city(N+1) is the goal city C_G. Every person starts in C_I and must reach C_G;
; every plane starts in C_I and must end in C_G.
;
; - fly takes (timeTerre ?from ?to) time units and adds (citythreat ?to) to the
;   total cost when the plane lands. citythreat is 0 for C_I and C_G.
; - A plane carries at most one person: (libre ?a) holds while it is empty.
; - board and debark are instantaneous. Under PDDL 2.1 epsilon-separation a plan
;   with k actions on its critical path ends at M + O(k * epsilon), where M is the
;   sum of the flight durations on that path. ZenoSolver reports M, i.e. the
;   makespan in the limit epsilon -> 0.
;
; See README.md, section "PDDL".

(define (domain multi-zeno-travel)
  (:requirements :typing :durative-actions :fluents)
  (:types city locatable - object
          aircraft person - locatable)

  (:predicates
    (at ?x - locatable ?c - city)
    (in ?p - person ?a - aircraft)
    (libre ?a - aircraft))

  (:functions
    (timeTerre ?from ?to - city)
    (citythreat ?c - city)
    (total-cost))

  (:action board
    :parameters (?p - person ?a - aircraft ?c - city)
    :precondition (and (at ?p ?c) (at ?a ?c) (libre ?a))
    :effect (and (not (at ?p ?c)) (in ?p ?a) (not (libre ?a))))

  (:action debark
    :parameters (?p - person ?a - aircraft ?c - city)
    :precondition (and (in ?p ?a) (at ?a ?c))
    :effect (and (not (in ?p ?a)) (libre ?a) (at ?p ?c)))

  (:durative-action fly
    :parameters (?a - aircraft ?from ?to - city)
    :duration (= ?duration (timeTerre ?from ?to))
    :condition (at start (at ?a ?from))
    :effect (and (at start (not (at ?a ?from)))
                 (at end (at ?a ?to))
                 (at end (increase (total-cost) (citythreat ?to))))))

fly lasts (timeTerre ?from ?to). Its only condition is that the plane is at ?from at the start, and it adds (citythreat ?to) to total-cost when it lands.
board and debark are instantaneous, and (libre ?a) holds while plane ?a is empty, which enforces capacity one.
The metric minimises total-time and total-cost together.

title: PDDL
text:
Problems
zeno pddl [instance options] [-O FILE] [--no-front]
The default file name is zeno<n>n<t>t<p>pMulti.pddl. A complete example, for \(n = 2\), \(t = 2\), \(p = 1\) (durations \((1, 2)\), costs \((2, 1)\) after the swap):
$ zeno pddl -n 2 -t 2 -p 1 -O example.pddl
(define (problem MULTIZENO-A)
  (:domain  multi-zeno-travel)
  (:objects plane1 - aircraft
            person1 person2 - person
            city0 city1 city2 city3 - city)
  (:init (= (total-cost) 0)
         (= (citythreat city0) 0)
         (= (citythreat city1) 2)
         (= (citythreat city2) 1)
         (= (citythreat city3) 0)
         
; city1
         (= (timeTerre city0 city1) 1)
         (= (timeTerre city1 city0) 1)
         (= (timeTerre city3 city1) 1)
         (= (timeTerre city1 city3) 1)
         (= (timeTerre city1 city2) 103)
         
; city2
         (= (timeTerre city0 city2) 2)
         (= (timeTerre city2 city0) 2)
         (= (timeTerre city3 city2) 2)
         (= (timeTerre city2 city3) 2)
         (= (timeTerre city2 city1) 103)
         
; plane init
         (at plane1 city0)
         (libre plane1)
         
; person init
         (at person1 city0)
         (at person2 city0)
         
)
(:goal (and 
         (at person1 city3)
         (at person2 city3)
         (at plane1 city3)
         ))
  (:metric (and (minimize (total-time)) (minimize (total-cost)))))

; Durations : 
; 1 2 
; Costs : 
; 2 1 
; Pareto points : Makespan - Cost
; 6 6
; 8 5
; 10 4
; 12 3

city0 is \(C_I\), city1…cityN the central cities, city(N+1) is \(C_G\); citythreat is the landing cost, 0 for both hubs.
timeTerre is written for both orders of every pair: \(d_i\) between \(C_I\) and \(i\), \(\bar d_i\) between \(C_G\) and \(i\), and \(\max(d_i, \bar d_i) + \max(d_j, \bar d_j) + 100\) between two central cities. Central flights are never faster than through a hub, so every problem satisfies (A1) when symmetric and (A1-NS) otherwise. They are written for every pair, so the file is quadratic in \(n\).
Every person and every plane starts in \(C_I\), and the goal puts all of them in \(C_G\).
The trailing comments list the durations (both sides when non-symmetric), the costs, and, for a symmetric instance without --no-front, the Pareto front as makespan cost lines. Note the order: makespan first, the reverse of zeno front’s cost makespan.

title: PDDL
text:
Plane goals
The goal requires every plane to end in \(C_G\) as well as every person. Problem files written before plane goals were added (pull request #9) only constrain the persons: planes may end anywhere, and the makespan is the last arrival. For symmetric instances under (A1) that variant has the same front (Theorem 4.9, machine-checked), so the fronts in old files remain valid. The Lean checker covers it too, for certificates of version 1 (Cert.check_sound_anywhere).

title: PDDL
text:
Makespan semantics
board and debark take no time in the model. Under the ε-separation of PDDL 2.1, a planner’s plan with \(k\) actions on its critical path ends at \(M + O(k\varepsilon)\), where \(M\) is the sum of the flight durations on that path. ZenoSolver reports \(M\), the makespan in the limit \(\varepsilon \to 0\). Statement 1.2 of the note argues the correspondence in both directions (a sketch, not formalised). Plans of the domain are event-ordered, and for those the front is the same (Corollary 6.10). Whether PDDL planners and VAL accept zero-duration actions is not checked.

title: PDDL
text:
Size
The writer is quadratic in \(n\), because of the central flights: about \(2n^2\) timeTerre lines. On an Apple M4 Max, a problem with \(n = 1000\) is written in 0.36 s and takes 46 MB. Without --no-front, zeno pddl also solves the instance first, which adds its solve time (size guidance).

title: Model and data files
Model and data files
Model and data files
text:
Data files
-d FILE reads the durations and costs from a file instead of the generator. -n must still be given and must match the file. Two layouts:
2 lines, symmetric: durations, then costs.
6 10
40 20
This is tests/golden/data/lpt-counterexample.dat: \(d = (6, 10)\), \(c = (40, 20)\). With -n 2 -t 5 -p 2 it is the smallest instance on which the 2016 greedy misses a front point (§5).
3 lines, possibly non-symmetric: \(C_I\)-side durations \(d\), \(C_G\)-side durations \(\bar d\), costs.
3 19
3 11
5 1
This is the instance of Proposition 6.5 (zeno -n 2 -t 7 -p 4 -d prop65.dat), on which waiting is harmful. A 3-line file with equal first and second lines is symmetric.
Reading rules (src/zeno/legacy_input.cpp):

tokens are separated by whitespace, and every non-blank line must have exactly \(n\) of them; blank lines are skipped, so a trailing newline or blank line is harmless (the golden instance trailing-newline checks it);
each token is read as an integer (std::stoi): 3.7 reads as 3, and a token that does not start with a number is an error;
the file must have 2 or 3 non-blank lines;
every value is then multiplied by -r (default 1) and truncated toward zero, as for generated instances, and negative values are rejected.

zeno generate writes the current instance in this format (command line).

title: Model and data files
text:
The 2016 swap






Warning



After reading or generating the vectors, if \(n > 1\) and the first duration exceeds the second, \(d_1 > d_2\), zeno exchanges the durations and the costs, and reverses the \(C_G\)-side durations. The 2016 code assumed increasing durations and did this, and zeno keeps it so that both build the same instance from the same options.


The rule, from legacy::buildInstance:
if(n > 1 && d[0] > d[1])
{
    std::swap(d, c);           // durations <-> costs
    std::ranges::reverse(de);  // C_G-side durations reversed
}
if(symmetric)
    de = d;
Consequences:

2-line file. A file 5 3 / 1 2 is solved as durations \((1, 2)\) and costs \((5, 3)\). zeno front prints a note on stderr when this happens to a data file:
zeno: note: the first duration exceeds the second, so the duration and cost lines of FILE were swapped, as the 2016 solvers did (order the cities to avoid it)
zeno pddl and zeno generate apply the same swap without the note.
3-line file. The swap is worse: \(d\) and \(c\) are exchanged and \(\bar d\) is reversed, so each city gets another city’s \(C_G\)-side duration. The file 5 3 / 7 8 / 1 2 becomes \(d = (1, 2)\), \(\bar d = (8, 7)\), \(c = (5, 3)\).
The generator. It computes durations on decreasing arguments, so for an increasing generating function the first duration is the largest and the swap fires. Then -C sets the durations and -D the costs (generator). This is why the default instances have \(d_i = i\) and \(c_i = n + 1 - i\).
Ties. After truncation the first two durations may be equal, and then nothing is swapped. -n 10 -D 1 (log, -r 1) gives \(d = (2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0)\) and \(c = (1, \dots, 10)\), whereas -n 10 -D 1 -r 100 swaps and gives \(d = (100, 200, \dots, 1000)\). The meaning of -C and -D thus depends on -r.
Round trips. zeno generate writes the instance after the swap. If that instance still has \(d_1 > d_2\), reading the file back swaps it again.

To avoid the trap, order the cities by duration so that \(d_1 \le d_2\) (any order of the others is fine), and check the instance with zeno generate ... -d FILE before solving it.

title: Lean tools
text: The Lean 4 project in lean/ (library ZenoFront) formalizes the theory note and ships two executables. Both are compiled Lean programs whose central function carries a kernel-checked theorem. Installation explains how to build them; the blueprint maps every statement of the note to its Lean declarations.

title: Lean tools
text:
zeno-check: the verified checker
lake exe zeno-check FILE     # or lean/.lake/build/bin/zeno-check FILE
It reads a certificate of either version and prints one of two verdicts:

accepted: … (exit code 0): the checking function returned true. The message names the theorem that backs it and the scope of the claim, for example
accepted: the 6 points are the Pareto front (all gaps relaxed: for every central flight table; ZenoFront.Cert.check_sound)
accepted: the 9 points are the Pareto front of all feasible plans (version 2, fastest relaxed, 0 roles, 0 lagrangian, 6 balanced and 2 search gap(s), the others relaxed: for every central flight table satisfying A1-NS; ZenoFront.Cert2.check_sound)
(the second is the instance of Proposition 6.5);
rejected: <reason> (exit code 1): the file is malformed or an obligation fails.

Only accepted is backed by the theorem. The reasons are diagnostics, recomputed outside the verified function.
What it verifies:



Version
Gap kinds
Fastest point
Soundness theorem




1 (symmetric)
relaxed, forest
closed form \(2 d_{\min} \lceil s/p \rceil\)
Cert.check_sound: if check accepts, the listed points are exactly the Pareto front of every feasible plan, for every table of central flights satisfying (A1), or every table if all gaps are relaxed. Cert.check_sound_rat extends it to plans with rational times, Cert.check_sound_anywhere to planes ending anywhere (PDDL without plane goals).


2 (non-symmetric)
relaxed, roles, lagrangian, balanced, search
closed, relaxed, roles, balanced, search
Cert2.check_sound: the same for every feasible plan; under (A1-NS) when a kind other than relaxed is used. search rests on Theorem 6.9 for every plan (schedulableDomination_all). When a certificate lists EO, the checker also tests that every listed plan is event-ordered (Cert2.check_sound_EO).



For forest gaps the Lean checker computes \(E\) with the σ-DP over the non-dominated cities, or with the tree DP when it estimates that cheaper (useTreeDP); it proves only the lower-bound direction, which is all soundness needs. The C++ checker uses the link-forest DP. Both are exact and agree on every sample.

title: Lean tools
text:
zeno-front: the verified solver
lake exe zeno-front FILE     # or lean/.lake/build/bin/zeno-front FILE
It reads an instance from the header of FILE, that is the lines instance n t p, d …, dbar … and c … of a certificate (an optional zeno-certificate line first, and anything after c ignored). It prints the Pareto front as cost makespan lines by increasing cost, as zeno front does. It needs symmetric durations and \(1 \le p \le t\), and otherwise stops with an error (exit code 1). Any certificate written by zeno is a valid input:
zeno -n 10 -t 8 -p 3 --certificate inst.cert > /dev/null
lake exe zeno-front inst.cert
The front is ZenoFront.solveFront d c t p. By solveFront_isParetoFront, under (S) and (A1) with \(1 \le p \le t\), it is exactly the Pareto front of the feasible plans. The solver finds the levels where \(E\) drops by splitting intervals between \(d_{\min}\lceil s/p\rceil\) and \((2t-p)\,d_{\max}\). At each level it takes \(L(T)\) when the bracket \(L(T) \le E(T) \le U_2(T)\) closes, and otherwise runs the link-forest DP or the σ-DP, whichever is estimated cheaper. Both are proved equal to \(E(T)\) (Theorem 7.5, Theorem 7.6).
It is slower than zeno, but it needs no certificate and no trust in the C++ code. On the 66 suite instances it finishes every one within 60 s with the same front as zeno front (results).

title: Lean tools
text:
Trust base
What a verdict of zeno-check, or a front of zeno-front, relies on:

The Lean kernel and three axioms. Every theorem of ZenoFront is checked by the kernel and depends only on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. The axiom audit (lake env lean scripts/CheckAxioms.lean) enforces this over every declaration of the library, and rejects sorryAx and Lean.ofReduceBool (native_decide). CI runs it on every change. The blueprint badges come from the same check (collectAxioms) on the listed declarations.
The definitions. A theorem is only as good as the match between its definitions and the intended mathematics. For the checker these are Feasible, planCost, planMakespan, achievable and IsParetoFront (§1.2, §1.5). Plans may fly central-to-central legs of any duration dc, wait anywhere and hand passengers over anywhere; planes must end in \(C_G\) in Cert.check_sound (Cert.check_sound_anywhere lifts this for version 1); forest gaps assume (A1) on dc, and the version 2 kinds other than relaxed assume (A1-NS).
The parser. parseAnyCert and the main of ZenoCheck.lean / ZenoFrontMain.lean are outside the verified statement: the theorems are about the parsed values, so a parser bug could make the checker verify a different front than the file’s. The parser only translates numbers and 1-based indices; it mirrors readCertificate in src/zeno/certificate.cpp.
The compiler. lake exe zeno-check runs the checking function as compiled code, so its verdict also trusts the Lean compiler and runtime, not only the kernel. To avoid that, a certificate can be checked by the kernel with decide +kernel, as lean/ZenoFront/Examples.lean does for two small certificates (§5). That is practical for small certificates only.

The listed plans of a certificate are re-simulated by the checker, so a solver bug in building plans can only cause a rejection. Theorem 4.1, the achievability construction, is not needed for soundness. It is machine-checked anyway, and it is what makes zeno-front’s points achievable.

title: C++ library
text:
Everything zeno does is in the static library zeno_core (CMake alias zeno::core), whose public headers are in include/zeno/. The command line (src/zeno/main.cpp) is a thin wrapper around it. There are no install rules: use the library from a CMake project with add_subdirectory (or FetchContent), then
The library needs C++23. Namespace zeno; errors are reported by exceptions (std::invalid_argument for invalid input, std::runtime_error for I/O and parse errors).

title: C++ library
C++ library
text:
Types

zeno/types.hpp
Cost and Time are std::int64_t. Durations are in the instance’s time unit; the solver works with half makespans \(T\), so a symmetric plan at level \(T\) has makespan \(2T\) (times the gcd of the durations). kInfCost (a quarter of the largest int64) stands for “no solution”, isInf(x) tests for it, and addCost(a, b) is saturating addition.


zeno/instance.hpp

Instance

d (durations \(C_I \leftrightarrow i\)), dbar (durations \(C_G \leftrightarrow i\), equal to d when symmetric), c (landing costs), t, p. n() is the number of cities, landings() is \(s = 2t - p\), symmetric() tests d == dbar, and validate() throws unless \(1 \le p \le t\), \(n \ge 1\), the vectors have length \(n\) and every value is non-negative. Central-to-central flights are not part of an instance: they are assumed no faster than through a hub (A1).

FrontPoint, Front

A point {cost, makespan}, ordered by <=>; a front is a std::vector<FrontPoint> sorted by increasing makespan, hence strictly decreasing cost.

paretoFilter(points)

Keeps the points that no other point weakly dominates (one per distinct objective vector), sorted by increasing makespan.




zeno/plan.hpp

Leg, Plan

A leg is {from, to, depart, arrive, passenger}. Locations are 0 for \(C_I\), 1…\(n\) for the central cities (city \(i\) of the instance is location \(i+1\)) and \(n+1\) for \(C_G\); passenger is \(-1\) when the plane flies empty. A plan is the legs of every plane, in order.

checkPlan(instance, plan) -> PlanCheck

Simulates a plan against the model of the theory note, sharing no code with the plan builder: every plane starts in \(C_I\) at time \(\ge 0\), chains its legs with exact durations and ends in \(C_G\); there is no \(C_I\)–\(C_G\) flight and central-to-central legs are rejected; every passenger rides a time-ordered chain of legs from \(C_I\) to \(C_G\); a leg carries at most one passenger. Returns ok, the first violated rule in error, the cost and the makespan.

buildPlan(instance, reduced, forest)

The plan of Theorem 4.1 for a link forest: every plane drops one passenger per child edge, flies its filler as alternating crossings, then picks up the passenger its parent dropped, waiting if needed.

mirrored(instance), mirrorPlan(plan, n)

The instance with \(C_I\) and \(C_G\) exchanged, and the time reversal of a plan, which turns plans where every plane picks up at most once into plans where every plane drops off at most once.

title: C++ library
text:
Entry points

Symmetric fronts: zeno/solve.hpp

solveFront(instance, options = {}) -> SolveResult

The exact Pareto front of a symmetric instance. Throws std::invalid_argument for an invalid or non-symmetric instance. SolveResult holds front, plans (with options.plans, plans[i] realises front[i] and was checked by checkPlan) and stats.


SolveOptions is shared by both entry points:








Field
Default
Meaning




threads
0
Worker threads; 0 for all hardware threads.


plans
false
Also build and check a plan for every front point.


levels
Automatic
LevelStrategy::Sweep (bracket every level, then the exact DP on the open ones), Search (bisect for the breakpoints of \(E\)), or Automatic (sweep up to \(2^{12}\) levels, search beyond).


table
Automatic
Layout of the one-plane table: dense or staircase, chosen by size.


roleStates
2,000,000
Non-symmetric: states of the balanced role program per level.


roleWork
50,000,000
Non-symmetric: transitions of the balanced role program per level.


refineSeconds
30
Non-symmetric: time after which the refinement of open gaps stops.


searchWork
20,000,000
Non-symmetric: work limit of the exact gap search, per gap.




SolveStats

The level range (lowestLevel, highestLevel, scale, levels), reducedCities, maxTree, how levels were settled (closedByBracket, closedByPairs, closedByChains, closedByMonotonicity, exactCalls), the DP work (work.states, work.relaxations) and the time per phase. zeno --stats prints them (command line).




Non-symmetric brackets: zeno/ns.hpp

solveBracket(instance, options = {}) -> BracketResult

A certified bracket of the front of any valid instance (for symmetric ones prefer solveFront). upper lists points achieved by simulated plans, and plans the plans with options.plans. For the gap between upper[i] and upper[i + 1], gapLower[i] bounds the cost of every plan with makespan below upper[i + 1].makespan, and gapProof[i] says how; fastestLower and fastestProof rule out faster plans. exact() is true when the fastest makespan is certified and every gap closed; assumptions() lists "A1-NS" when a closed gap needs it. For an open gap, openReason[i] is Incomplete (a limit was reached) or Unscheduled (a cheaper balanced configuration exists, but no schedule found fits the gap).

GapProof

Relaxed (lemma R with role weight \(\min(2d, 2\bar d)\): no assumption on central flights), Roles (role relaxation), Lagrangian (Lagrangian relaxation of the per-city balance), Balanced (the cheapest balanced role configuration), Search (exhaustive search over role configurations with exact schedules). All but Relaxed need (A1-NS): Roles, Lagrangian and Balanced through Theorem 6.1, Search through Theorem 6.9, which covers every plan. Open marks a gap that no bound closes.




Certificates: zeno/certificate.hpp

Certificate

version (1 or 2), the instance, assumptions ("S", "A1", "A1-NS"), the front by increasing makespan, one plan per point, one GapBound per gap, Lagrangian multipliers (v2), and the fastest bound (v2). Format.

makeCertificate(instance, result)

The version 1 certificate of a solved front (requires SolveOptions::plans). A gap gets relaxed when \(L\) reaches the cost, forest otherwise.

makeBracketCertificate(instance, bracket)

The version 2 certificate of an exact bracket (requires exact() and SolveOptions::plans); throws std::invalid_argument otherwise.

writeCertificate(out, certificate), readCertificate(in)

Text I/O. The reader throws std::runtime_error with the line number on a syntax error, and refuses values above \(2^{36}\), \(n\), \(t\), \(p\) above \(10^5\) and more than \(10^7\) legs.

checkCertificate(certificate) -> CertificateCheck

The reference checker: ok, every failed obligation in errors, and in relied the assumptions the accepted obligations needed. It uses the library’s own dynamic programs for the gap bounds, so it is a consistency check, not an independent proof; the Lean checker is the independent one (Lean tools).




Instances and files: zeno/legacy_input.hpp, zeno/io.hpp

legacy::Options, legacy::buildInstance(options, &swapped)

The instance options of the 2016 solvers and the 2016 construction, quirks included: values multiplied by adjust (-r) and truncated toward zero, and the swap of durations and costs when d[0] > d[1]; swapped reports whether it happened. Unlike the 2016 code it accepts \(t = p\). Formulas on the generator page.

writePddlProblem(out, instance, front = nullptr), defaultPddlName(instance)

The PDDL problem for pddl/multi-zeno-travel.pddl, with the front appended as comments when given (PDDL), and the 2016 default name zeno<n>n<t>t<p>pMulti.pddl.

writeDataFile(out, instance)

The data file read by -d: 2 lines if symmetric, 3 otherwise.

cli::parseInstanceArguments(args), cli::instanceOptionsHelp(), cli::integerValue(flag, value)

The command-line parser for the instance options (it consumes -n -t -p -d -C -D -E -W -r -j -k   -l -m -x -y and drops -F, leaving the other tokens in rest), its help text, and integer parsing with an error naming the flag.

title: C++ library
text:
Internals
These headers are public, for the tests and benchmarks; their interfaces may change.



Header
Content




zeno/reduce.hpp
ReducedInstance and reduce(instance): dominated and equal cities merged (Proposition 7.9), durations divided by their gcd, role weights (fill, drop, pick, low) for non-symmetric instances, lowestLevel() and highestLevel() (Proposition 7.10), maxTree() \(= \min(p, t-p+1)\). Kept cities of a symmetric instance form a staircase: \(d\) strictly increasing, \(c\) strictly decreasing.


zeno/one_plane.hpp
OnePlaneTable(d, c, maxLandings, maxLevel, layout): \(G[m][T]\), the cheapest \(m\) landings within \(T\) (Lemma 7.2), dense or as Pareto staircases (memory independent of the magnitude of the durations); paretoPoints, witness.


zeno/forest.hpp
relaxedCost (the relaxation \(L\), lemma R), ForestProgram / forestCost (link forests with trees of at most maxTreePlanes planes: 2 gives \(U\), 3 gives \(U_3\), maxTree() gives \(E\) exactly, Theorem 7.5), LinkForest and ForestPlane, LevelStats.


zeno/breakpoints.hpp
breakpoints(lo, flo, hi, fhi, f, threads): the breakpoints of a non-increasing function by parallel interval splitting, \(O(r \log(hi - lo))\) evaluations for \(r\) breakpoints.


zeno/roles.hpp
Role configurations (RoleConfig), the exact balanced program BalancedRoles (DP over planes on the imbalance vector, Proposition 6.6; gives up beyond its state and work limits), RoleRelaxation, lagrangianRoles / lagrangianValue, scheduleRoles.


zeno/ns_search.hpp
Template schedules (Lemma 6.3): templateMakespan, templatePlan; exactSchedule (every drop-off order and matching of one configuration); searchGap (the exhaustive gap search of Corollary 6.10).


zeno/parallel.hpp
workerCount(requested) and parallelFor(count, threads, body), dynamic scheduling, first exception rethrown.



Doxygen documentation of all headers is built by the doc target, with -DZS_BUILD_DOC=ON.

title: Installation and build
text: ZenoSolver has two independent parts. The C++ solver zeno and its library compute fronts and write certificates. The Lean 4 project in lean/ holds the formalization, the verified checker zeno-check and the verified solver zeno-front. Neither needs the other to build. The end-to-end tests use both.

title: Installation and build
text:
The C++ solver

Requirements

CMake ≥ 3.21;
a C++23 compiler: GCC ≥ 13, Clang ≥ 16 or Apple Clang ≥ 15;
optionally Doxygen, for the API documentation (ZS_BUILD_DOC).

The solver has no other dependency. The benchmarks fetch Google Benchmark v1.9.1 when they are enabled.


Build with the presets
cmake --preset release
cmake --build --preset release
ctest --preset release
The binaries go to build/<preset>/, so zeno is build/release/zeno. Without presets:
cmake -S . -B build/default && cmake --build build/default -j
The presets are defined in CMakePresets.json:








Preset
Configuration
Purpose




release
CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
Optimised build with link-time optimisation. Tests included.


dev
Debug, CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON
Debug build with compile_commands.json.


asan
RelWithDebInfo, ZS_SANITIZERS=address;undefined
AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer; any report fails the test.


bench
ZS_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON, ZS_BUILD_TESTS=OFF
Release build of the component benchmarks and zeno, without the tests.



Each configure preset has a build preset of the same name, and release, dev and asan have a test preset. To build the solver alone, without the tests, the oracle and the golden suite:
cmake --preset release -DZS_BUILD_TESTS=OFF
cmake --build build/release --target zeno


Options
Set with -D<option>=<value> at configure time (CMakeLists.txt):








Option
Default
Meaning




ZS_BUILD_TESTS
ON
Build the tests, the brute-force oracle and the golden suite.


ZS_BUILD_FUZZERS
OFF
Build the libFuzzer targets (clang only; combine with ZS_SANITIZERS).


ZS_BUILD_BENCHMARKS
OFF
Build the component benchmarks; fetches Google Benchmark v1.9.1.


ZS_BUILD_DOC
OFF
Add the doc target (requires Doxygen).


ZS_ENABLE_IPO
ON
Link-time optimisation in Release builds, when supported.


ZS_NATIVE
OFF
Tune for the build machine (-march=native). Binaries are not portable.


ZS_SANITIZERS
empty
Sanitizers to enable, e.g. address;undefined.


ZS_WARNINGS_AS_ERRORS
OFF
Treat compiler warnings as errors.





Targets



Target
What it is




zeno
The command-line solver (command line).


zeno_core (alias zeno::core)
The static library behind it (C++ library).


zenoOracle
The brute-force oracle that produced the golden fronts (tests/oracle), with ZS_BUILD_TESTS.


ut-zeno-core, ut-oracle, ut-pddl
Unit and property tests, with ZS_BUILD_TESTS.


fuzz-certificate-replay, fuzz-certificate
Replay of the fuzzing corpus (with the tests), and the libFuzzer target (with ZS_BUILD_FUZZERS).


bm-core, bm-plan, bm-ns
Component benchmarks, with ZS_BUILD_BENCHMARKS (results).





Tests
ctest --preset release runs the golden suite and the unit tests. The golden tests compare the front of zeno with fronts computed by the brute-force oracle, and check that zeno check accepts the certificate of each (golden suite). ut-zeno-core compares the exact solver with a second, independent oracle (tests/oracle/partitionEnum.hpp) on random instances, and checks metamorphic properties: permuting cities, or adding dominated or duplicate cities, changes nothing; scaling durations or costs scales the front; adding \(a\) to every cost adds \(s \cdot a\) to every front cost. ut-zeno-core <trials> <maxN> <maxT> <maxP> <maxS> runs a larger sweep.
The certificate reader and checker are fuzzed (tests/fuzz/fuzz_certificate.cpp). CTest replays the seed corpus on every platform, and CI runs libFuzzer with ASan and UBSan for two minutes on every pull request:
cmake -S . -B build/fuzz -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++ \
      -DZS_BUILD_FUZZERS=ON -DZS_SANITIZERS="address;undefined"

title: Installation and build
text:
The Lean project
The toolchain is pinned: Lean v4.36.0 and Mathlib v4.36.0 (lean/lean-toolchain, lean/lakefile.toml, lean/lake-manifest.json). Install Lean with elan, then, from lean/:
lake exe cache get        # download the Mathlib build cache (never build Mathlib from source)
lake build --wfail        # build ZenoFront; warnings, including `sorry`, are errors
lake env lean scripts/CheckAxioms.lean   # axiom audit
lake build zeno-check     # the compiled checker (first build compiles Mathlib's C code, ~1.5 min)
lake build zeno-front     # the verified solver
bash test/run.sh          # check the test certificates against their expected verdicts
The executables are written to lean/.lake/build/bin/. The Mathlib cache takes several gigabytes. When a second checkout of the repository already has it, copying lean/.lake/packages from there (copy-on-write, cp -c on APFS) avoids a second download; lake build then compiles only ZenoFront.
The axiom audit fails if any declaration of a ZenoFront module uses an axiom other than propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound; in particular it rejects sorryAx and native_decide (Lean tools).

End to end
From the repository root, with both parts built:
# certificates of the golden and random instances, accepted by both checkers
bash lean/test/e2e.sh build/release/zeno lean/.lake/build/bin/zeno-check

# zeno-front against zeno front on the golden, quick and three regime instances
bash lean/test/front.sh build/release/zeno lean/.lake/build/bin/zeno-front "$(mktemp -d)" \
  "tests/golden/instances.txt|tests/golden/data" "bench/instances/quick.txt|bench/instances/data" \
  "lean/test/front-regimes.list|bench/instances/data"

title: Installation and build
text:
Continuous integration
Every pull request is built and tested on Linux (GCC, Clang) and macOS, and once more under the sanitizers (.github/workflows/ci.yml). .github/workflows/lean.yml builds the Lean project, runs the axiom audit, a grep for sorry and admit, and the end-to-end checks, on every push and pull request that touches lean/** or the C++ solver. .github/workflows/bench.yml runs the benchmarks (results).

title: Installation and build
text:
This website
The site is a Quarto project in site/, rendered into docs/, which GitHub Pages serves from master. With Quarto, a TeX distribution (for the PDF) and a built Lean project:
bash site/build.sh             # regenerate the blueprint and the tables, render into docs/
bash site/build.sh --no-lean   # reuse site/lean-status.json instead of querying Lean

title: ZenoSolver
text:
MultiZenoTravel is a bi-objective planning benchmark: \(p\) planes carry \(t\) passengers from an initial city \(C_I\) to a goal city \(C_G\) through \(n\) central cities, and every plan has a total cost (landing fees) and a makespan. ZenoSolver computes the exact Pareto front of an instance, so that multi-objective planners can be scored against the true front.
zeno prints the front as cost makespan lines by increasing cost. It is exact for symmetric durations, which includes every instance the generator emits. For non-symmetric durations it prints a certified bracket, and says whether the bracket closes into the exact front.

title: ZenoSolver
text:
How it works
The front is the set of breakpoints of \(E(T)\), the least cost of an admissible partition of the \(2t-p\) landings into \(p\) groups whose durations each sum to at most \(T\) (Proposition 7.1). zeno brackets \(E\) between a relaxation \(L\) and the pairs and chains bounds \(U\), \(U_3\) on every level, and runs the exact link-forest dynamic program only where the bracket leaves a level open. The algorithm page has the details, and the theory note the proofs.
The 2016 ZenoSolver, published with the EvoCOP 2015 paper, scheduled each fixed multiset of landings greedily, and that greedy is not optimal (§5). The current solver replaces it and reproduces every golden front of an exhaustive oracle, including those on which the 2016 solvers were wrong.
