title: ZenoSolver
text:
What is proved
The blueprint has 63 nodes. 21 are machine-checked theorems and 7 are Lean definitions. 13 have formalised parts, and 22 are not in Lean. The library has 3,675 declarations (2,112 theorems) in 42 modules (Lean v4.36.0, Mathlib v4.36.0). Apart from propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, no declaration uses another axiom: no sorry and no native_decide.
The front theorem is machine-checked for every instance with symmetric durations and central flights no faster than through a hub, assumptions (S) and (A1) (Corollary 4.8). So are the exactness of both dynamic programs (Theorem 7.5, Theorem 7.6), the verified solver zeno-front (solveFront_isParetoFront) and the soundness of the certificate checker zeno-check, symmetric (Theorem 9.1) and not (version 2). For non-symmetric instances the note proves schedulable domination (Theorem 6.9, machine-checked). The exhaustive search over role configurations that closes the gaps left by harmful waiting (Proposition 6.5) rests on it.






Who did what. The model and the first algorithms are those of the original papers, Quemy & Schoenauer (EvoCOP 2015) and Quemy, Schoenauer & Dréo (arXiv:2304.14659, 2023). The current solver, the theory note that corrects the papers, the Lean 4 formalization and this website are the work of Alexandre Quemy. On the blueprint, the papers’ statements are reproduced verbatim in grey boxes with their attribution; blue and green boxes hold the note and the Lean development.

title: ZenoSolver
text:
Explore

Solver: installation, command line, C++ library, certificate format, Lean tools, algorithm.
Instances: model and data files, generator, PDDL, benchmark and golden suites, instances with known fronts, size guidance.
Blueprint: every statement of the theory note, with the papers’ versions, the Lean declarations and a status badge from #print axioms. Also as a PDF.
Claim graph and history: the claims, their dependencies and statuses, rebuilt from the knowledge commits, and the replay of those commits.
Experiments: the experiment campaign (in preparation).
Results: timings and fronts on every suite instance, computed from the committed baselines.
About: the papers, attribution, and what the note corrects.

title: Command line
text:
zeno [front] [instance options] [--threads N] [--levels MODE] [--plans] [--certificate FILE] [--stats]
zeno check CERTIFICATE
zeno pddl [instance options] [-O FILE] [--no-front]
zeno generate [instance options] [-O FILE]
The first argument selects the command; without one, zeno runs front. -h or --help anywhere prints the help below, which is the output of the current build (regenerated with the site). An unknown option is an error.
Exit codes: 0 on success; 1 on an error (the message on stderr starts with zeno:); 2 when zeno check rejects a certificate.

title: Command line
text:
Instance options
All four commands but check build an instance from the same options, those of the 2016 zenoSolver, and build the same instance from them, quirks included. The generator page gives the formulas, and the model page the data file formats.








Option
Default
Meaning




-n N
3
Central cities.


-t N
3
Passengers.


-p N
2
Planes, \(1 \le p \le t\). Unlike the 2016 solvers, \(t = p\) is accepted.


-d FILE
—
Data file: durations then costs (2 lines, symmetric), or CI-side durations, CG-side durations, costs (3 lines). Every line has \(n\) integers. Overrides the generator.


-C K
3
Cost generator: 1 log, 2 sqrt, 3 identity, 4 power of two, 5 staircase.


-D K
3
Duration generator, same codes.


-E K, -W K
—
Non-symmetric durations: -E generates the CI-side durations, -W the CG-side ones. Both are needed; -D is then ignored.


-r R
1
Multiply every value by \(R\) before truncating it to an integer.


-j, -k
1, 0
Scale and translation of the cost generator’s argument.


-l, -m
1, 0
Scale and translation of the duration generators’ argument.


-x, -y
1, 0
Scale and translation of the output of every generator.


-F
—
Accepted for compatibility and ignored: the front is always printed.



-n, -t, -p, -C, -D, -E, -W and -r take integers; -j, -k, -l, -m, -x and -y take decimal numbers.






The 2016 swap



After building the vectors, if \(n > 1\) and the first duration exceeds the second, the durations and the costs are exchanged (and the CG-side durations reversed), as the 2016 code did. This always happens with the default generator, and to any data file whose first duration is the larger. front prints a note on stderr when it happens to a data file. See the swap trap.

title: Command line
text:
front: the Pareto front
zeno -n 2 -t 3 -p 2
4 8
6 6
8 4
One cost makespan line per front point, by increasing cost (so by decreasing makespan). Costs and durations are integers, and so is every makespan.
Symmetric instances (durations to \(C_I\) and to \(C_G\) equal, every generated instance without -E/-W): the front is exact. A zeno instance has no central-to-central flights; the front is that of the model in which they exist but are no faster than through a hub, assumption (A1), as in every PDDL file zeno writes (Corollary 4.8 with Proposition 7.1). When every gap of the front is closed by the relaxation \(L\), the same front holds for central flights of any duration; the certificate then lists only relaxed gaps.
Non-symmetric instances (-E/-W, or a 3-line data file with different lines): zeno computes a certified bracket (algorithm). Stdout lists the points achieved by simulated plans, and stderr reports which gaps between them a lower bound closes:
zeno -n 4 -t 3 -p 2 -E 3 -W 2 -r 10 > front.txt
non-symmetric instance: 12 achieved points; fastest makespan certified; 11 of 11 gaps certified; the front is exact, assuming A1-NS
When the fastest makespan is certified and every gap is closed, the printed points are the exact front, under the listed assumption (A1-NS) when a bound needs it. Otherwise the report says the front is a bracket and lists each open gap:
  open gap between makespans M1 and M2: a plan with makespan < M2 costs at least B (achieved: C; REASON)
where the reason is either “a cheaper balanced configuration exists, no schedule found within the gap” or “the exact balanced program gave up” (a limit of SolveOptions was reached, below).

Solver options

--threads N

Worker threads for the level evaluations. Default 0: all hardware threads.

--levels MODE

How the levels \(T\) (half makespans, in units of the gcd of the durations) are visited. sweep brackets every level between \(T_{\rm lo}\) and \(T_{\rm hi}\), then runs the exact DP on the open ones. search bisects for the breakpoints of \(E\), which evaluates \(O(r \log(T_{\rm hi} - T_{\rm lo}))\) levels for \(r\) breakpoints. auto (the default) sweeps when the range has at most \(2^{12}\) levels and searches beyond. Use search for wide level ranges, for example durations scaled by a large -r.

--plans

After the front, print a plan for every point, each checked by simulation (checkPlan). One block per point, from the cheapest, then one line per plane, legs as from->to[depart,arrive] with pK when passenger \(K\) is aboard. Locations are CI, c1…cn and CG.


# cost 6, makespan 6
plane 1: CI->c1[0,1]p1 c1->CI[1,2] CI->c2[2,4]p2 c2->CG[4,6]p2
plane 2: CI->c2[0,2]p3 c2->CG[2,4]p3 CG->c1[4,5] c1->CG[5,6]p1
Here plane 1 drops passenger 1 in city 1 and returns empty, and plane 2 picks that passenger up on its way back to \(C_G\).

--certificate FILE

Write a certificate of the front to FILE (format): version 1 for symmetric instances, version 2 for non-symmetric ones. A non-symmetric front gets a certificate only when its bracket is exact; otherwise zeno stops with no certificate: the front is a bracket with open gaps. Implies building the plans.

--stats

Print solver statistics on stderr:


levels 2..4 (x1, 3 levels), cities 2, max tree 2
settled: bracket 3, pairs 0, chains 0, monotone 0, exact 0
work: 5 states, 105 relaxations
seconds: table 4.084e-06, bracket 3.9708e-05, chains 0, exact 0, plans 6.6083e-05

levels: the range \([T_{\rm lo}, T_{\rm hi}]\) of scaled half makespans, the gcd the durations were divided by (x), and the number of levels in the range;
cities: cities left after the dominance reduction; max tree: \(\min(p, t-p+1)\), the largest useful link tree;
settled: how the value of each evaluated level was established. bracket when \(L = U\); pairs when \(U\) is exact (trees of at most 2 planes); chains when \(U_3\) settles it; monotone when \(E\) takes equal values at both ends of an interval; exact counts the link-forest DP evaluations;
work: DP cells written and candidate transitions examined, summed;
seconds: time in the one-plane table, the bracket, the chains bound, the exact DP and the plans.

title: Command line
text:
check: verify a certificate
zeno -n 2 -t 5 -p 2 -d tests/golden/data/lpt-counterexample.dat --certificate lpt.cert
zeno check lpt.cert
certificate accepted, assuming S
zeno check reads a certificate of either version and verifies the four obligations of the format. On success it prints the assumptions the accepted obligations needed (S: symmetric durations; A1: central flights no faster than through a hub, needed by forest gaps; A1-NS for the version 2 kinds other than relaxed). On failure it prints one error: line per failed obligation, then certificate rejected, and exits with code 2.
zeno check reuses the solver library’s dynamic programs for the gap bounds, so it is a consistency check of the solver, not an independent proof. The Lean checker zeno-check is the independent one.

title: Command line
text:
pddl: write a PDDL problem
zeno pddl -n 10 -t 8 -p 3            # writes zeno10n8t3pMulti.pddl
zeno pddl -n 10 -t 8 -p 3 -O p.pddl --no-front
Writes the instance as a PDDL 2.1 problem for the domain pddl/multi-zeno-travel.pddl (PDDL page). The default file name is zeno<n>n<t>t<p>pMulti.pddl, the 2016 one; -O FILE sets it. For a symmetric instance the front is solved and appended as comments, unless --no-front. Non-symmetric problems are written without a front.

title: Command line
text:
generate: write a data file
zeno generate -n 4 -t 3 -p 2 -C 2 -D 2 -r 10
10 14 17 20
20 17 14 10
Writes the instance that the options describe as a data file for -d: durations then costs for a symmetric instance, or CI-side durations, CG-side durations, costs otherwise. Without -O FILE it writes to standard output. -t and -p are validated but not written.
The output is the instance after the 2016 swap. Reading it back with -d gives the same instance only if its first duration does not exceed its second; otherwise the swap applies again. A data file 5 3 / 9 1 is solved as durations 9 1 and costs 5 3, generate writes it that way, and reading that back gives 5 3 / 9 1 again. Order the cities by increasing duration (the swap trap).

title: Command line
text:
Limits of the non-symmetric bracket
The non-symmetric bracket stops some of its searches at limits set in zeno::SolveOptions (include/zeno/solve.hpp). The command line uses the defaults; the library can change them.








Field
Default
Limits




roleStates
2,000,000
States of the exact balanced role program, per level.


roleWork
50,000,000
Transitions of the exact balanced role program, per level.


refineSeconds
30
Time after which the refinement of open gaps stops; the remaining gaps stay open, with their lower bounds.


searchWork
20,000,000
Work of the exhaustive gap search (role configurations with exact schedules), per gap.



A gap left open by a limit is reported as such (the exact balanced program gave up). It is not an error: the printed points are still achieved by simulated plans, and the reported lower bounds are still proved.

title: Command line
text:
Values and limits

Durations, costs and times are non-negative integers (std::int64_t). The instance is validated: \(n \ge 1\), \(1 \le p \le t\), every vector of length \(n\), every value non-negative.
The certificate reader refuses values above \(2^{36}\), \(n\), \(t\) or \(p\) above \(10^5\), and more than \(10^7\) legs, so no sum in the checker can overflow.
For sizes and running times, see the size guidance.

title: Certificate format
text:
A certificate lists one plan per front point and one lower bound per gap between consecutive points. A checker that verifies its four obligations has proved that the list is the Pareto front, without trusting the solver (Theorem 9.1). zeno --certificate FILE writes one, zeno check FILE verifies it (command line), and so does the Lean checker zeno-check, whose acceptance is backed by a kernel-checked soundness theorem (Lean tools).
The rest of this page is doc/certificate-format.md, the specification both checkers follow, included as it stands in the repository.

title: Certificate format
text:
A small certificate
zeno -n 2 -t 5 -p 2 -d tests/golden/data/lpt-counterexample.dat --certificate lpt.cert writes, for \(d = (6, 10)\), \(c = (40, 20)\), \(t = 5\), \(p = 2\):
zeno-certificate 1
instance 2 5 2
d 6 10
dbar 6 10
c 40 20
assume S
front 6
320 48
280 56
260 60
240 64
200 72
160 80
plan 1 2
plane 1 …
…
lower-bounds 5
…
end
The points are listed by increasing makespan. assume S only: every gap of this front is closed by the relaxation \(L\), so the certificate holds for central flights of any duration. Both checkers accept it:
$ zeno check lpt.cert
certificate accepted, assuming S
$ lake exe zeno-check lpt.cert
accepted: the 6 points are the Pareto front (all gaps relaxed: for every central flight table; ZenoFront.Cert.check_sound)

title: Certificate format
text:
The specification
zeno --certificate FILE writes, next to the front, a certificate that a checker can verify without trusting the solver. The reference checker is zeno check FILE; the Lean checker in lean/ (in progress) reads the same format. This page defines the format and what a checker must verify. The proofs behind each obligation are in doc/theory/exact-front.md.

What a certificate proves
For an instance with symmetric durations and a front \((C_1, M_1), \dots, (C_r, M_r)\) with \(M_1 < \dots < M_r\) and \(C_1 > \dots > C_r\), the certificate shows that this list is exactly the Pareto front:

Achieved. For every \(i\), the plan given for point \(i\) is feasible and has cost \(C_i\) and makespan \(M_i\). The checker simulates it.
Nothing is faster than \(M_1\). \(M_1 = 2\, d_{\min} \lceil s/p \rceil\), where \(s = 2t - p\). Every plan has at least \(s\) segments (counting lemma), some plane flies at least \(\lceil s/p \rceil\) of them, and under (S) each lasts at least \(2 d_{\min}\).
Nothing in a gap is cheaper. For every \(i < r\), every plan with makespan \(< M_{i+1}\) costs at least \(C_i\). Such a plan has \(\lfloor M/2 \rfloor \le h = \lfloor (M_{i+1} - 1)/2 \rfloor\); with \(g\) the gcd of the durations, its groups fit in level \(T = \lfloor h / g \rfloor\) of the instance with durations divided by \(g\) (for a front point \(M_{i+1} = 2gT_{i+1}\), so \(T = T_{i+1} - 1\)). As \(E\) and \(L\) are non-increasing, it suffices that the bound at level \(T\) is at least \(C_i\). The certificate names how the checker establishes this bound:

relaxed: recompute the relaxation \(L(T)\) (no admissibility). Lemma R gives \(\text{cost} \ge L(\lfloor M/2 \rfloor)\) for every plan under (S) alone, whatever the central flights.
forest: recompute \(E(T)\) with the link-forest dynamic program (trees of at most \(\min(p, t-p+1)\) planes). This relies on the converse theorem, hence on (A1).

Nothing is cheaper than \(C_r\). \(C_r = s \cdot c_{\min}\): every plan lands at least \(s\) times.

Then every plan \((C, M)\) is weakly dominated by a listed point: \(M \ge M_1\) by 2; if \(M_i \le M < M_{i+1}\) then \(C \ge C_i\) by 3; if \(M \ge M_r\) then \(C \ge C_r\) by 4. Together with 1, the list is the front.
A certificate whose gap bounds are all relaxed is valid for every symmetric instance, without assumption (A1).


Syntax
A text file of lines. Blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored. Tokens are separated by spaces. All numbers are non-negative integers.
zeno-certificate 1
instance <n> <t> <p>
d <d_1> ... <d_n>
dbar <dbar_1> ... <dbar_n>
c <c_1> ... <c_n>
assume <assumption>...
front <r>
<C_1> <M_1>
...
<C_r> <M_r>
plan <i> <p>
plane <k> <m>
<from> <to> <depart> <arrive> <passenger>
...
lower-bounds <r - 1>
<i> <kind>
...
end

d: durations between \(C_I\) and each central city; dbar: between \(C_G\) and each central city; c: landing costs.
assume: the assumptions the solver used. Version 1 knows S (symmetric durations, i.e. d = dbar) and A1 (central flights at least as long as through a hub). A checker refuses an obligation that needs an assumption the certificate does not list.
front: the points by increasing makespan.
plan <i> <p>: the plan of point \(i\) (1-based), for the \(p\) planes, in order \(i = 1..r\). Each plane <k> <m> (k = 1..p, in order) is followed by its \(m\) legs, in flight order.
A leg: locations are 0 for \(C_I\), 1..n for the central cities, n+1 for \(C_G\); times are integers; passenger is 1..t, or 0 when the plane flies empty.
lower-bounds: one line per gap \(i = 1..r-1\), in order, with its kind, relaxed or forest.
Limits of the reference reader: every number at most \(2^{36}\), \(n, t, p \le 10^5\), at most \(10^7\) legs in all.



Plan semantics (obligation 1)
A plan is feasible when:

every plane starts in \(C_I\) at time \(\ge 0\); each leg leaves the location where the previous one arrived, no earlier than that arrival; each leg is a flight between a hub (\(C_I\) or \(C_G\)) and a central city, lasting d (via \(C_I\)) or dbar (via \(C_G\)) — there is no \(C_I\)–\(C_G\) flight, and version 1 has no central-to-central legs; every plane ends in \(C_G\);
every passenger \(1..t\) starts in \(C_I\) at time 0 and rides a chain of legs, each leaving where the previous one arrived and no earlier, ending in \(C_G\);
a leg carries at most one passenger (by construction of the format).

Boarding and debarking take no time. The cost is the sum of c over the legs that land in a central city; the makespan is the last arrival.


Example
zeno -n 2 -t 5 -p 2 -d tests/golden/data/lpt-counterexample.dat --certificate lpt.cert writes a certificate for the instance \(d = (6, 10)\), \(c = (40, 20)\), \(t = 5\), \(p = 2\), whose front has six points; zeno check lpt.cert verifies it.


Version 2: non-symmetric instances
zeno --certificate FILE on a non-symmetric instance writes a version 2 certificate when its bracket is exact (every gap closed). Version 2 differs from version 1 in four places.

The header is zeno-certificate 2, and dbar may differ from d. assume lists S only for symmetric durations, and A1-NS when a bound below needs it (Theorem 6.1 of the theory note: every plan is weakly dominated by a role configuration with the same cost and loads at most its makespan, if central flights are useless).
Levels are in units of the gcd g of all durations, and are full loads: a crossing \(C_I \to i \to C_G\) or back weighs \(d_i + \bar d_i\), a drop-off \(2 d_i\), a pick-up \(2 \bar d_i\). A plan of makespan \(< M_{i+1}\) fits in level \(T = \lfloor (M_{i+1} - 1)/g \rfloor\). (For symmetric durations, version 1’s half-loads and level \(\lfloor (M_{i+1}-1)/(2g) \rfloor\) are kept.)
A line fastest <kind> after the front names the bound that rules out plans faster than \(M_1\): the bound at level \(\lfloor (M_1 - 1)/g \rfloor\) must be infinite. Kinds: closed (symmetric only, as in version 1), relaxed, roles, balanced, search.
Gap kinds, in addition to relaxed (lemma R with weight \(\min(2d_i, 2\bar d_i)\) per landing, no assumption) and forest (symmetric, A1):

roles (A1-NS): each plane flies an odd number \(\ge 1\) of crossings and its other landings weigh at least \(\min(2d, 2\bar d)\); all loads add up to the crossing weight of the landings, so the largest is at least that over \(p\).
lagrangian mu_1 ... mu_n (A1-NS): with one signed integer multiplier per city, a drop-off in \(i\) costs \(c_i + \mu_i\) and a pick-up \(c_i - \mu_i\); the balance of drop-offs and pick-ups city by city drops out and the planes decouple. Every \(\mu\) gives a lower bound, so the checker only evaluates the bound at the listed \(\mu\).
balanced (A1-NS): the checker reruns the exact program over balanced role configurations (a branch and bound against the cost \(C_i\)) and requires that it finishes.
search (A1-NS): the checker reruns the exhaustive search over role configurations of cost below \(C_i\) with exact schedules (every order of drop-offs, matching and pick-up order) and requires that none finishes before \(M_{i+1}\). By Corollary 6.10 (schedulable domination, Theorem 6.9) this rules out every feasible plan, also on instances with a city of \(d = \bar d = 0\). Older certificates may list the assumption EO (event-ordered plans) for such instances. Both checkers still read it, but it is no longer needed. This is the only kind that closes gaps opened by harmful waiting (Proposition 6.5). It is also a valid fastest kind.


Obligations 1 and 4 are unchanged. The reference checker (zeno check) reads both versions. The Lean checker (lean/) verifies version 1. Of version 2 it verifies the relaxed, roles, lagrangian, balanced and search gaps, and fastest closed, relaxed, roles, balanced and search. Its soundness theorem Cert2.check_sound is about every feasible plan, with or without a city of \(d = \bar d = 0\) (schedulableDomination_all, lean/README.md). When a certificate lists EO, the Lean checker also tests that every listed plan is event-ordered, and the points are then also the front of the event-ordered plans (Cert2.check_sound_EO).

title: Algorithm
text: This page summarises how zeno computes a front. The proofs are in the theory note (§7 for the symmetric algorithm, §6.5 for the non-symmetric one), and each step links to its node of the blueprint.

title: Algorithm
text:
The reformulation
A plan lands at least \(s = 2t - p\) times in central cities (Lemma 3.2). Under (S) and (A1), the front is reached by plans with exactly \(s\) landings, split among the planes as an admissible partition (Corollary 4.8): a partition \(X_1, \dots, X_p\) of a multiset \(X\) of cities with a parity matrix, that is, in every connected component of the plane–city graph, an even number of planes land an even number of times (Definition 2.2, Lemma 2.4). An admissible partition is flown with no waiting, in makespan \(2\max_k \delta(X_k)\) where \(\delta\) sums the durations (Theorem 4.1), and no plan does better (Theorem 4.7).
With integer durations divided by their gcd \(g\), let \[E(T) = \min\{c(X) : |X| = s,\ X_1,\dots,X_p \text{ admissible},\ \delta(X_k) \le T\ \forall k\}.\] \(E\) is non-increasing, and the front is the set of its breakpoints, \((E(T), 2gT)\) wherever \(E(T) < E(T-1)\) (Proposition 7.1). Only the levels \(T_{\rm lo} = d_{\min}\kappa \le T \le T_{\rm hi} = d_{\rm cheap}\kappa\) matter, with \(\kappa = \lceil s/p \rceil\) (Proposition 7.10): below, there is no plan; above, \(E\) is the cheapest cost \(s\,c_{\min}\).

title: Algorithm
text:
Symmetric pipeline

Reduce. Divide the durations by their gcd, merge equal cities and drop dominated ones (\(d_{i'} \le d_i\) and \(c_{i'} \le c_i\)), which changes neither \(E\) nor the front (Proposition 7.9). The kept cities form a staircase: durations strictly increasing, costs strictly decreasing (reduce, zeno/reduce.hpp).
One-plane table. \(G[m][T]\), the cheapest \(m\) landings whose durations sum to at most \(T\) (Lemma 7.2). It is stored densely when small, otherwise as one Pareto staircase of (load, cost) per \(m\), so that memory does not depend on the magnitude of the durations (OnePlaneTable).
Bracket each level. Three knapsacks over planes and landings combine gadgets:

\(L(T)\): single planes of any size, no admissibility. It is a lower bound on the cost of every plan of makespan at most \(2T\), whatever the central flights (lemma R, Lemma 3.4);
\(U(T)\): single planes of odd size, and pairs, two planes of even size linked at a city;
\(U_3(T)\): in addition, chains of three planes.

\(L \le E \le U_3 \le U\) (Proposition 7.3). \(E = U\) when useful link trees have at most two planes, \(q_{\max} = \min(p, t-p+1) \le 2\), and \(E = U_3\) when \(q_{\max} \le 3\) (Proposition 7.4). A level is settled when the bracket closes.
Exact DP on the open levels. On the levels where \(L < U_3\), the link-forest DP computes \(E(T)\) exactly (Theorem 7.5). A partition is admissible iff it has a link forest (Lemma 2.6): a forest on the planes whose edges carry city labels, each edge \(\{u, v\}\) labelled \(i\) using one landing in \(i\) of both \(X_u\) and \(X_v\), such that every plane keeps an odd number of free landings (Definition (link forest)). In the plan, a link at \(i\) is a passenger dropped off in \(i\) by one plane and picked up by the other. Trees have at most \(q_{\max}\) planes (Corollary 2.7). The DP roots every tree and combines child subtrees as Pareto staircases over \((\tau, \text{cost})\), \(\tau\) being the part of a plane’s load taken by its child edges, so its work depends on the staircase sizes and not on \(T\) (ForestProgram, zeno/forest.hpp). Because \(E\) is non-increasing, equal values at both ends of an interval fix it on the whole interval (monotone in --stats).
Find the breakpoints. --levels sweep evaluates every level; --levels search splits every interval \((a, b)\) with \(E(a) > E(b)\) at up to threads evenly spaced levels evaluated in parallel. Pieces with equal ends are constant, so with \(r\) breakpoints it evaluates \(O(r \log(T_{\rm hi} - T_{\rm lo}))\) levels (breakpoints, zeno/breakpoints.hpp). The default, auto, sweeps up to \(2^{12}\) levels and searches beyond, which is why the time grows with the logarithm of the level range.
Plans. For each point, the partition is rebuilt from the exact method’s choices, a link forest computed from it, and the plan of Theorem 4.1 built. Every plane first drops off one passenger per child edge (\(C_I \to b \to C_I\)), then flies its free landings as alternating crossings, then picks up the passenger its parent dropped (\(C_G \to a \to C_G\)). Every plan is re-simulated by checkPlan, which shares no code with the builder.
Certificate. Each gap gets relaxed when \(L\) already reaches the cost at the level below the next point, forest otherwise (certificate format).

Why the 2016 solvers were wrong: they fixed the multiset of landings (a PPP) and scheduled it greedily, longest first onto the least-loaded plane. That is a heuristic, and deciding whether a fixed multiset can be flown within a makespan is strongly NP-complete (§5, Theorem 8.1). The link-forest DP does not fix the multiset. Its cost is pseudo-polynomial (Corollary 8.3).

title: Algorithm
Algorithm
text:
Complexity
From §8 of the note, with \(\hat m = s - p + 1\) (the largest group) and \(q_{\max} = \min(p, t-p+1)\):







Step
Time




One-plane table \(G\), all levels
\(O(n\,\hat m\,T_{\rm hi})\)


\(L\) and \(U\), per level
\(O(p\,s^2 + n\,\hat m^2)\)


\(U_3\) chains, per level
\(O(n^2\,\hat m\,s + p\,s^2)\)


Link-forest DP, per level
\(O(n\,q_{\max}^2 s^2 T + p\,q_{\max} s^2)\)


Plan for one point
\(O(s + n + p)\), up to union–find



These are the bounds of the dense algorithm. The staircase representations make the table and the forest DP independent of the magnitude of the durations in practice, and the breakpoint search evaluates \(O(r \log(T_{\rm hi} - T_{\rm lo}))\) levels instead of all of them. Measured scaling is on the results and size guidance pages.

title: Generator
text:
Construction
For cities \(i = 1, \dots, n\), with \(r\) = -r, \((j, k)\) = -j -k, \((l, m)\) = -l -m and \((x, y)\) = -x -y (defaults \(r = 1\), \(j = l = x = 1\), \(k = m = y = 0\)):

Costs on increasing arguments, durations on decreasing ones: \[c_i = x\,f_C(\lfloor j\,i + k \rfloor) + y, \qquad d_i = x\,f_D(\lfloor l\,(n+1-i) + m \rfloor) + y.\] With -E and -W (both needed; -D is then ignored), \(d_i\) uses \(f_E\) and the \(C_G\)-side \(\bar d_i = x\,f_W(\lfloor l\,(n+1-i) + m \rfloor) + y\).
Every value is multiplied by \(r\) and truncated toward zero: \(v \leftarrow \operatorname{trunc}(r\,v)\). -r 100 keeps slowly growing functions such as \(\ln\) from collapsing onto a few integers.
The swap. If \(d_1 > d_2\), durations and costs are exchanged and \(\bar d\) is reversed (model). For increasing functions on decreasing arguments \(d_1 > d_2\) holds unless truncation makes the first two values equal. So in practice:

(the floors inside \(f\) are left out for readability). After the usual swap, durations increase with \(i\) and costs decrease: faster cities cost more, which is what makes the front non-trivial.






Non-symmetric options that give a symmetric instance



After the swap, the \(C_I\)-side durations come from -C and the \(C_G\)-side ones from -W. When the two functions coincide the instance is symmetric, whatever -E says. -n 3 -E 1 -W 3 (with the default -C 3) is symmetric, and zeno solves it as such. Use a -W different from -C, for example -E 3 -W 2:
$ zeno generate -n 4 -t 3 -p 2 -E 3 -W 2 -r 10
10 20 30 40
10 14 17 20
40 30 20 10

title: Generator
text:
The families in the suites
The families suite runs every family on \(n = 10\), \(t = 8\), \(p = 3\) (suites): linear (-C 3 -D 3), log (-C 1 -D 1 -r 100), sqrt (-C 2 -D 2 -r 100), pow2 (-C 4 -D 4), staircase (-C 5 -D 5 -r 10), and the mixed log-linear and sqrt-linear. The default family is the only one with a closed-form front (known fronts). The others need the general algorithm, and on them the 2016 greedy can miss points.
Every instance the generator builds without -E/-W is symmetric, and every PDDL problem zeno writes from it satisfies (A1), so its front is exact.

title: Size guidance
text:
What drives the time
From the algorithm (algorithm) and the measurements:

The number of landings \(s = 2t - p\) and the largest group \(\hat m = s - p + 1\) set the size of the one-plane table and of the knapsacks of the bracket, \(O(p\,s^2 + n\,\hat m^2)\) per level. This is the main cost on the large instances above: \(t\) matters more than \(n\).
The level range \(T_{\rm hi} - T_{\rm lo} = (d_{\rm cheap} - d_{\min})\kappa\) multiplies the per-level cost under --levels sweep. Under search (automatic beyond \(2^{12}\) levels), the solver evaluates \(O(r \log(T_{\rm hi} - T_{\rm lo}))\) levels for \(r\) front points, so scaling the durations costs little: \(10^8\) levels take about 4 ms (BM_SolveLargeDurations).
The number of front points \(r\): one plan per point with --plans or --certificate, and a certificate grows with the plans (\(3.9\) MB and 240,000 legs for \(n = 100\), \(t = 60\), \(p = 10\)).
The cities after reduction. Dominated and equal cities are merged first, so many cities with few distinct (duration, cost) pairs cost little. The default family keeps every city.
Links. The exact link-forest DP runs only on levels the bracket leaves open, and only when link trees can have three planes or more, \(q_{\max} = \min(p, t - p + 1) \ge 3\). Its cost grows with \(q_{\max}^2\). On default-generator instances such as -n 200 -t 100 -p 10, --stats reports every level settled by the bracket (\(L = U\)) and no exact DP call.

--threads parallelises the level evaluations; --stats shows where the time goes (command line).

title: Size guidance
text:
Non-symmetric instances
The non-symmetric bracket is much more expensive. The exact balanced role program has a state space growing like \((2n)^{t-p}\), and the gap search enumerates role configurations with every order and matching. Both stop at limits (2,000,000 states and 50,000,000 transitions per level, 20,000,000 search steps per gap, 30 s of gap refinement; SolveOptions). Beyond them zeno reports the open gaps with their lower bounds instead of an exact front. The instance of Proposition 6.5 (\(n = 2\), \(t = 7\), \(p = 4\)) closes in a few milliseconds. Keep \(t - p\) small for exact non-symmetric fronts.

title: Size guidance
text:
The Lean tools

zeno-check on the certificate of a suite instance takes 26 ms at the median and 2.1 s at most (3.9 MB, \(n = 100\), \(t = 60\), \(p = 10\)). The σ-DP it uses for forest gaps is exponential in the number of cities that survive the dominance merge. When that is large it switches to the tree DP, and certificates of -n 40 -t 20 -p 8 -C 2 -D 2 -r 100 take 12.5 s.
zeno-front is slower than zeno: 10 s for \(n = 100\), \(t = 60\), \(p = 10\), against 61 ms. It finishes all 66 suite instances within 60 s (results).

title: Claim graph
text:
Every result of the theory note is a claim in the registry claims.toml, and every change to its status is a Conventional Knowledge Commit: a commit whose type (proof, formalize, conjecture, refute, lit, …) and footers (Status:, Depends-On:, Closes:, Disproves:) record what it asserts and what it rests on (CONTRIBUTING.md). The graph below is rebuilt from those commits when the site is built.
The graph has 57 claims, 27 Lean declarations that close them and 2 refutations, joined by 23 Closes, 80 Depends-On, 2 Disproves edges. By effective status, the claims are 23 machine-checked, 28 proof in the note, 4 conjectured, 2 disproved. The replay has 59 knowledge commits, all of 2026-11-24; the other 210 commits of the history (features, fixes, documentation) are left out.
A node’s colour is its effective status: the weakest of its own status and of everything it depends on, so an open or refuted claim colours every result that rests on it. Click a node to trace its dependencies; press Play, or drag the slider, to replay the knowledge commits in order.

title: Claim graph
text:
How it is built
site/gen_graph.py reads the history with claimgraph and keeps only the knowledge commits, those whose type belongs to a CKC profile. The other commits (features, fixes, documentation) would add a node per scope and a replay step each, with no claim status to show, so the graph and its replay are compacted to the knowledge commits. The registry claims.toml gives each claim its statement and Lean declarations. claimgraph status . --claims claims.toml prints the same statuses from the command line.

title: About
text:
What the note corrects
The note’s §5 and §6 and the draft erratum (doc/erratum.md) give the details. In short:

The per-PPP greedy is not optimal
Both papers fix a multiset of landings (a PPP) and schedule it greedily, longest flights first onto the least-loaded plane (EvoCOP 2015 Algorithm 1, arXiv §3.2), and claim the result is the optimal makespan of that PPP. It is not. On \(d = (6, 10)\), \(c = (40, 20)\), \(t = 5\), \(p = 2\) the 2016 solver misses the front point (260, 60) (§5). That front is checked by the Lean kernel alone (Examples.lptCounterexample_front). No polynomial per-PPP rule can be exact unless P = NP: deciding whether a multiset of landings can be flown within a makespan is strongly NP-complete (Theorem 8.1).


Proposition I holds only for the front
“Pareto-optimal plans use exactly \(2t - p\) central cities” is false for plans: with zero costs, a plan with more landings can be Pareto-optimal. What holds is the front statement: the front is the Pareto set of \((c(X), M(X))\) over multisets \(X\) of \(2t - p\) landings, with \(M(X)\) the least makespan of an admissible partition of \(X\) (Corollary 4.8, machine-checked).


Waiting can be harmful in the non-symmetric case
The arXiv paper’s non-symmetric argument assumes that no plane has to wait harmfully for a passenger. That is false, even with no central flights and under the triangle inequality (Conjecture 6.5, refuted; Proposition 6.5). The note replaces the assumption with schedulable domination (Theorem 6.9, machine-checked for every plan). An exhaustive search over role configurations with exact schedules is therefore sound, and zeno uses it to close such gaps.


The pairing argument without (A1) is incomplete
Without (A1), the arXiv pairing argument concludes “lower cost” from a set inclusion and “dominates” from per-pattern durations; both steps fail (Conjecture 4.10, open). Without (A1) the front is still certified wherever the relaxation \(L\) meets the achieved cost, which covers every front of the default generator (Theorem 10.1).


What still holds
The model, the flight patterns, the lower bound of \(2t - p\) landings, and the no-waiting construction of a plan from an admissible partition (Theorem 4.1, machine-checked). On the default generator the front is known in closed form, and the published benchmark fronts of that family are probably right despite the greedy (Conjecture 10.2, checked on 115 instances, not proved).

title: About
section: Honesty: what is proved, and how
text:
Honesty: what is proved, and how
The blueprint has 63 nodes. 21 are machine-checked theorems and 7 are Lean definitions. 13 have formalised parts, and 22 are not in Lean. The library has 3,675 declarations (2,112 theorems) in 42 modules (Lean v4.36.0, Mathlib v4.36.0). Apart from propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, no declaration uses another axiom: no sorry and no native_decide.
The blueprint’s badges are computed when the site is built, from collectAxioms on the Lean declarations each node lists. A node is badged machine-checked only if the declarations that formalise its whole statement are axiom-clean theorems. Declarations covering only part of a statement are listed under it, with their own badges, and the node keeps the note’s status. The generator stops if a declaration is missing or a label is not found in the note.
The compiled tools add trust in the Lean compiler and in an unverified parser (trust base).
